<![CDATA[Irish Times Feeds]]>https://www.irishtimes.comWed, 04 Nov 2026 21:24:13 +0000en1hourly1<![CDATA[Gambling regulator tackles ‘dozens’ of black market players]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/04/four-out-of-10-using-online-accounts-for-sport-betting-go-on-to-other-forms-of-gambling/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/04/four-out-of-10-using-online-accounts-for-sport-betting-go-on-to-other-forms-of-gambling/Wed, 04 Nov 2026 12:30:00 +0000

The State’s gambling watchdog has tackled “dozens” of black market betting businesses since new laws took effect this year.

The Gambling Regulatory Authority of Ireland (GRAI) began licensing online bookies this year under legislation that overhauled how the industry is governed.

The regulator has acted against “dozens of unlicensed operators” since July, GRAI chief executive Anne Marie Caulfield said on Wednesday.

“They ranged from small Irish bookmakers to major online operators to the two largest prediction markets in the world,” Caulfield told reporters.

The regulator’s powers range from issuing “cease and desist” letters to High Court action.

Caulfield, who did not name individual businesses, indicated that most unlicensed players halted operations after receiving initial cease and desist warnings.

“We have not been to the High Court,” she said.

Many black market operators ignore the legal safeguards applied to licensed businesses, including a ban on the use of credit cards and age checks, Caulfied pointed out.

The authority has also begun fielding complaints from punters through its consumer protection division, with many relating to difficulty getting money from online bookies.

The Gambling Regulation Act, 2024 requires licensees to respond promptly to customers’ requests for payment and to close accounts, Caulfield said.

Demand for drug treatment services has ‘exploded’, support group says

Gamblers complain that it is easier to open online betting accounts and deposit cash than it is to close them or withdraw funds, according to a GRAI-commissioned survey published by the Economic and Social Research Institute (ESRI) on Wednesday.

Researchers “did not drill into what the issues were”, according to ESRI head of behavioural research Pete Lunn. But he said gamblers found “a clear asymmetry” between depositing and withdrawing cash and opening and closing accounts.

Almost four in 10 people who open online accounts initially to bet on horse racing or sport go on to other forms of gambling, including casino games, slot machines and lotteries, the research shows.

Online betting companies cross-sell casino and slot machine games to these customers. Lunn argued that this drew them to forms of gambling where customers had a higher risk of developing problems.

He acknowledged that all companies with online operations legitimately used apps to make more money, but cautioned that it was important to establish where gambling businesses risked “crossing the line”.

Private security patrolling Dublin would not have additional capacity to arrest people

Most regular gamblers have more than one online account, the study shows. Around 10 per cent of the 1,000 people surveyed said they had four or more.

One in seven said emails or app notifications prompted their most recent gambling session, which some receive every day. Of their most recent session, 26 per cent of online punters said they had lost a lot of money, against 17 per cent of those who were betting in person.

One quarter were trying to reduce their gambling or wanted to do so, but one third of that group were betting the same amounts or more than a year previously.

Most gamblers feel positive about betting, the survey shows. Lunn acknowledged that most do not experience harm.

Licensed betting businesses will have to contribute to a social impact fund that the GRAI aims to establish next year. The authority is working with the market’s bigger players on a self-exclusion system for people who fear they have a problem.

The Irish Bookmakers Association welcomed the report, saying it had always insisted that regulation should be based on evidence.

The ESRI published Patterns of Online and In-person Gambling in Ireland by Deirdre Robertson, Diarmaid Ó Ceallaigh, Shane Timmons and Pete Lunn, on Wednesday.

]]>William West<![CDATA[Midterm elections ‘blue wave’ sends global stocks surging either side of the Atlantic]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/04/midterm-elections-blue-wave-sends-global-stocks-surging-either-side-of-the-atlantic/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/04/midterm-elections-blue-wave-sends-global-stocks-surging-either-side-of-the-atlantic/Wed, 04 Nov 2026 18:42:44 +0000Global stocks either side of the Atlantic surged following the “blue wave” of Democratic Party victories in the US midterm elections Thursday, as investors looked past political upheaval and promises of policy change to bet heavily on key drivers of economic growth.

Shares in Europe hit two-month highs, with its relations with the United States appearing to enter a new, more open era. Closer to home, nutrition group Glanbia grew its revenue and raised its guidance on earnings.

DUBLIN

The Iseq All-Share index rose 3.48 per cent to 14.852.83 by the close of markets. Glanbia led the charge, up 11.82 per cent to €22.04 a share after it announced a rise in revenue for the first nine months of the year, backed by strong consumer demand in protein and energy-based products. It also raised its guidance on full-year earnings per-share growth.

Bank of Ireland saw its share price jump 6.75 per cent to €19.45 a share, with rival AIB following behind, up 5.82 per cent to €11.55 a share by the end of trading hours after it raised forecasts for net interest income and customer loan growth.

Ryanair was up 5.73 per cent to close at €25.27 a share, somehow still flying high after it announced a 15 per cent fall in profits on Monday, amounting to €2.15 billion, although the airline’s chief executive Michael O’Leary committed the company to expanding next year, with the possibility of higher air fares.

LONDON

The London Stock Exchange saw sizeable increases in share prices for household brand names, although losses in the energy sector pulled the city’s two leading indices closer towards neutral. The blue-chip FTSE 100 increased 1.83 per cent, while the mid-cap FTSE 250 grew 0.98 per cent.

Supermarket giant M & S jumped 6.40 per cent after the company’s midyear fiscal results showed a strong rebound in profitability. Meanwhile, Associated British Foods, a grocery group that also has Penneys/Primark in its portfolio, followed behind, up 6.37 per cent after it returned a 63p per share dividend to shareholders.

But oil and gas companies Ithaca and BP suffered declines, down 7.90 per cent and 3.00 per cent, respectively. A mix of political uncertainty in the US and falling oil prices from the Middle East led investors to rethink their stake in the energy market.

EUROPE

Elsewhere in Europe, shares across the Continent surged, driven by strong investor confidence in safe bets across the banking and motor sectors. The blue-chip Stoxx 50 index jumped 2.09 per cent to a two-month high, while the mid-cap Stoxx 600 followed slightly behind, up 1.91 per cent by close of markets.

Germany’s Deutsche Bank jumped 6.88 per cent and Spain’s Banco Santander was up 4.87 per cent, while France’s BNP Paribas followed along, increasing 4.67 per cent, as traders sought low-risk, high-return investments to calm their nerves against election jitters and the AI boom.

BMW was up 5.50 per cent, with Mercedes Benz increasing 4.56 per cent, following strong earnings reports published earlier in the day upgrading the companies’ investment guidance.

NEW YORK

Early trades on Wall Street saw stocks rise and the dollar drop following the Democratic Party’s sweeping electoral victories across Congress, gaining control of the House of Representatives and the Senate.

The major stock indices – The S&P 500, the Nasdaq 100 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average – all hovered around a 2 per cent increase before 11am New York Time.

Investors appeared willing to look past the political upheaval, betting the main drivers of US growth, from consumer spending to the artificial intelligence boom, would remain intact. Political gridlock could curb further fiscal expansion and ease pressure on bonds, offering support for stocks.

While Democratic gains could complicate data centre development in some states, many investors see little immediate threat to the broader artificial intelligence investment picture. – Additional reporting: Bloomberg.

]]>Michael Nagle<![CDATA[Punter-friendly sports results hit revenue at Flutter’s Irish and British business]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/markets/2026/11/04/paddy-power-owner-flutter-pauses-share-buy-backs-to-focus-on-cutting-costs-and-debt/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/markets/2026/11/04/paddy-power-owner-flutter-pauses-share-buy-backs-to-focus-on-cutting-costs-and-debt/Wed, 04 Nov 2026 15:34:20 +0000Punter-friendly sports results hit revenues at Paddy Power owner Flutter‘s Irish and British business in the three months to the end of September, but online gaming boosted the division, figures show.

Betting giant Flutter lost $1.15 billion (€1 billion) in the three months to September 30th, including an $873 million charge for an online gambling ban in Brazil, the group said on Wednesday.

Revenues from betting on horse racing, football and other sports in the New York-listed giant’s UK and Ireland division slipped almost 7 per cent to $309 (€275 million) over the three months, from $330 million during the same period last year, Flutter said on Wednesday.

The Irish betting giant blamed an “adverse swing in sports results”, that is a higher-than-usual number of teams and horses backed by its customers winning, for part of the revenue slide.

But overall revenues at the division, which includes Paddy Power, Betfair and Sky Bet, increased 4 per cent to $889 million, boosted by strong growth in online casino games.

Last month Flutter confirmed it would cut 240 jobs at its Dublin head office from a total of 1,400 across the Irish and UK business to counter increased British betting tax.

Globally, Flutter will pause a share buyback programme to ​prioritise investment, cutting debt and cost savings, its new chief executive, Dan Taylor, said on Wednesday, after the company reduced its profit forecast for a fifth successive quarter.

Flutter, the world’s largest online gaming company, has been forced to lower its profit expectations ​as higher regulatory costs, increased competition and strategy missteps slowed previously booming US growth.

Taylor, who took charge in October, ⁠said his four immediate priorities would be to build on the company’s US leadership position, capture ‌opportunities ‌in ​the nascent prediction market sector, increase value from its non-US portfolio and simplify the company’s operating model.

Flutter shares were 1.9 per cent lower in premarket ⁠trading in New York.

“Delivering against those priorities ​will require faster execution, tough decisions and disciplined ​investment,” Taylor said in a statement.

He told Reuters he was confident of deleveraging ‌the company’s balance sheet over the next ​12 to 18 months towards its target leverage range of two to 2.5 times earnings.

The ⁠company’s leverage ratio has risen to ⁠4.6 times earnings from ​2.2 18 months ago, before acquisitions in the US, Italy and Brazil.

Flutter, whose business includes US sports betting market leader FanDuel, also has a plan announced in August to save $500 million (€439.45 million) by 2029.

Just over two years ago, when Flutter promised up to $5 billion to shareholders, it had expected the US betting boom to more than double its core profit to $5 billion by 2027.

By the end of June, the buyback had returned $1.37 ‌billion to shareholders.

Flutter is now ⁠forecasting a 7 per cent fall in full-year core profit to $2.5 billion from the $2.66 billion flagged in August and $2.59 billion expected by analysts. The latest cut was due to ‌adverse sports results and a sports betting ban in Brazil.

Taylor said, however, that the underlying performance in the US was ahead of expectations. – Additional reporting: Reuters

]]>Spencer Platt<![CDATA[Central Bank to cut up to 140 roles as it seeks to shave its costs by €75m]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/04/central-bank-to-cut-up-to-140-roles-as-it-seeks-to-shave-its-costs-by-75m/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/04/central-bank-to-cut-up-to-140-roles-as-it-seeks-to-shave-its-costs-by-75m/Wed, 04 Nov 2026 17:03:52 +0000The Central Bank of Ireland has announced plans to reduce its workforce by between 120 and 140 people in a bid to help achieve cost savings of €75 million a year by 2030.

Some €26 million of that figure is to be achieved through a reduction in pay costs and would represent an 8 per cent cut in projected 2030 pay expenditure.

In June, The Irish Times revealed that the jobs cuts and other expenditure measures had been flagged to employees in an email from governor Gabriel Makhlouf, who was reappointed for a second seven-year term in March.

According to its annual report, at the end of 2025, the Central Bank employed 2,225 full-time equivalent staff. If 140 roles are cut this would amount to a reduction in staff numbers of about 6 per cent.

In spite of its employee numbers reducing by 38 last year on the level in 2024, the Central Bank’s payroll costs increased. Salaries and allowances paid to staff last year rose to €211 million, up from €200 in 2024.

Some 825 members of staff were classified as earning €100,000 or more, with Makhlouf the top earner on €342,239.

Staff numbers at the Central Bank have doubled since 2008, including employees of the formerly separate financial regulatory authority that was folded into the bank in 2010, as it devoted more resources to supervising a growing number of authorised firms.

Meanwhile, the bank has racked up losses – including shortfalls of €104.6 million last year and €795.4 million in 2024 – after an era of super profits generated by the bank in the wake of the financial crisis came to an end in 2022.

The financial regulator said the majority of the reduction in projected expenditure would be achieved through non-pay measures, including targeted IT investment, reductions in consultancy and contractor spend, and other efficiency initiatives.

The Central Bank said these moves would allow it to “adapt to a challenging external environment and to assume new legislative responsibilities”.

The Central Bank has launched a voluntary severance scheme and said it had “commenced engagement with its people and staff representatives”.

“The scheme (which will be in line with standard public service conditions) will support delivery of a lower cost trajectory in a cost-effective manner while maintaining operational effectiveness and delivering an organisation that is more agile in response to a rapidly changing environment,” a statement from the bank said.

The Banking & Payments Federation Ireland (BPFI) welcomed the measures announced by the Central Bank.

BPFI chief executive Brian Hayes, said: “At a time when there is a strong focus both in Ireland and across Europe on simplification and competitiveness, it is important that this ambition is reflected across the regulatory system. A strong and effective regulator remains essential, but this must go hand in hand with a continued focus on efficiency, proportionality and ensuring the regulatory framework supports Ireland’s competitiveness as a financial services centre.”

]]><![CDATA[Record €85bn tax take as Government spending continues to climb]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/04/record-85bn-tax-take-as-government-spending-continues-to-climb/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/04/record-85bn-tax-take-as-government-spending-continues-to-climb/Wed, 04 Nov 2026 16:30:43 +0000The Government collected a record €85 billion in tax in the 10 months to October but spending continues to rise at a worrying rate.

The latest exchequer returns, published by the Department of Finance, showed total tax revenue stood at €84.9 billion at the end of last month.

When receipts from the Apple tax case are stripped out, the total was €7.9 billion or 10.3 per cent ahead of the same time last year.

The strong performance was led by income tax, which generated €31 billion for the 10-month period, 8.4 per cent up on last year, reflecting the high level of employment.

Government coffers were also buoyed by strong corporate tax receipts, which took in €23.9 billion, 23.4 per cent ahead of last year.

The concentration of corporate tax receipts around a small number of US multinationals remains a significant risk for the exchequer.

Fiscal advisers point out the flaws but Government ignores them. What’s the point of Ifac?

In 2025, just three firms – Apple, Microsoft and Eli Lilly – accounted for 46 per cent of receipts from the business tax.

October is not a VAT-due month and only “modest” receipts were collected during the month, but on a cumulative basis, the sales tax generated €20.5 billion, 7.3 per cent up on the 2025 total at this stage.

Total gross voted expenditure to the end of October amounted to €93.6 billion, which was 7.4 per cent up on last year.

The Government has come under pressure to rein in spending and save more of its corporate tax windfall.

The Irish Fiscal Advisory Council has warned there will be close to €2 billion of overruns in this year’s figures compared with what was forecast last year.

Much of the overrun total stems from an overspend in health.

In a bid to rein in spending, the Government has adopted a new spending framework that pledges to keep the annual lift in expenditure inside a 6 per cent threshold.

“Today’s exchequer figures reflect an economy that is continuing to perform well, despite the external challenges and headwinds facing us both domestically and globally,” Minister for Finance Simon Harris said.

“The continued strength of our economy and public finances has given us the capacity to support families and businesses through Budget 2027, as well as allowing us to invest in our public services and take important steps to safeguard our future,” he said.

“At a time of considerable global uncertainty, it is more important than ever that we manage our public finances responsibly,” Harris said.

“That is why, on budget day, I announced that an additional €1 billion in tax receipts, above and beyond what is required by law, will be transferred into the Future Ireland Fund next year,” he said.

Fine Gael considers ‘AI dividend tax credit’ for businesses

Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers said: “The increase in expenditure to end-October reflects the Government’s commitment to strengthening public services.”

On corporate tax, Orla Gavin, head of tax at KPMG Ireland, warned that some of the year-to-date corporation tax surge was expected to unwind in November.

“November will therefore be crucial in distinguishing timing effects from the underlying trend in corporation tax receipts,” she said.

The department warned last month that some company payments expected this year would not now arrive until early next year.

Sasha Kerins, tax partner at Grant Thornton Ireland, said: “The resilience of the domestic economy is particularly noteworthy against a more difficult international backdrop, including renewed inflationary pressures across Europe.”

]]>Sam boal/Collins Photos<![CDATA[After the SuperValu cyberattack, might your smart fridge be the next target? ]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/technology/2026/11/04/after-the-supervalu-cyberattack-might-your-smart-fridge-be-the-next-target/https://www.irishtimes.com/technology/2026/11/04/after-the-supervalu-cyberattack-might-your-smart-fridge-be-the-next-target/Wed, 04 Nov 2026 12:41:50 +0000Do you feel differently about your smart fridge?

The high-tech home hub allows you to check what food you have in, suggest recipes, and manage the family calendar, should you be able to afford its not-insignificant price tag.

But this week’s cyberattack on Supervalu’s refrigeration systems might be forcing people to re-evaluate its position in their home.

Where could the next attack come from?

You might equally be eyeing your connected coffeemaker warily, worried about what it could be getting up to behind your back. You might consider unplugging the robot vacuum cleaner in case it goes rogue while you are out on the school run.

Jokes aside, the recent spate of attacks on seemingly harmless systems should give us pause for thought. The problem with many of these connected devices is that as soon as you hook anything up to the internet, it opens up a chink in your armour , no matter how hard we try to lock it down.

It is a trade-off that we might not be aware we are making at the time – but it is a common thread in the modern world. For the sake of convenience, we give up a little security. Even with the most diligent company in charge of maintaining the security of the appliances, there is always a risk that something will go wrong. And with the growth in artificial intelligence (AI), the chance of a previously undetected vulnerability rearing its head has suddenly been magnified.

You might wonder why hackers would want to attack a smart home device in the suburbs of Dublin. While we may not have thousands of euro of stock to destroy, or disposable income to pay out ransoms, we do have something that is valuable: our data. And that, as we know, is worth a lot of money in the right – or wrong – hands.

There is also the chance that our smart home devices, unpatched and open to exploitation, may be used as part of an attack on a high-value target.

In recent days, a joint operation between public and private partners in the tech industry took down a global botnet that had been hidden in set-top boxes across 200 countries. The botnet, which was placed on the devices before they were sold, surreptitiously used the set-top boxes and internet connections of those unlucky enough to have installed them in their homes.

This is not a new threat. Botnets have been carrying out large-scale attacks for years. One example: in 2016, the Mirai botnet took over up to 560,000 unsecured or weak cameras, printers, and DVR players and knocked out Twitter, Reddit, and Netflix, among others.

So what can we do to protect ourselves? Besides cutting off the connection, that is, although you could argue there is no compelling need to have an oven or coffee maker with an internet connection.

There is some help on the way from the bureaucrats, with various rules regarding security being implemented at an EU level, forcing manufacturers to adopt a secure-by-design approach. But we can’t rely on them to fully shield us from all the risks.

There are ways to protect ourselves: keeping up to date with software releases to patch up any security holes is a given;buying reputable brands rather than settling for cheap, unbranded technology from online marketplaces is another. Changing the default passwords on devices is another tip from security experts.

But we need to be aware of what could be coming down the line.

Anthropic recently warned of another threat: that AI models are becoming so smart and small in terms of storage requirements that they could copy themselves into places you might not suspect – such as your smart fridge.

That could create an army of smart botnets that could, in theory, be commanded to launch attacks without needing a data centre to run from. And, the experts argue, that would be one that is very difficult to battle, because there is no centralised point from where the attack has been launched.

Of course it is never as simple as it looks. The scenario proposed by Anthropic was a test rather than a real-world incident, and the end result – a model that replicates itself – is more of a ‘could’ than a ‘did’. The model didn’t have to break in as such, although we are often so lax about security on these connected devices that it wouldn’t have presented a huge barrier if that had been the case.

There are a few lessons to learn here.

Take the claims of AI companies about the power and potential of their technology with a grain of salt, for both good and bad.

But perhaps, to be safe, you might also consider limiting smart technology to the essentials. Sometimes the trade-off just isn’t worth it.

]]><![CDATA[AIB raises outlook after sharp rise in new lending]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/04/aib-raises-outlook-after-sharp-rise-in-new-lending/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/04/aib-raises-outlook-after-sharp-rise-in-new-lending/Wed, 04 Nov 2026 07:35:22 +0000AIB has raised its forecasts for net interest income and customer loan growth after new lending rose sharply in the first nine months of the year.

A trading update from the bank today showed total income rose 3 per cent in the nine-month period to the end of September. AIB’s net interest income was €2.87 billion, up 2 per cent compared to the first nine months of 2025, while other income was up 7 per cent.

Gross lending at the bank has grown by €4 billion to €76.3 billion since the end of last year, representing an increase of 5.6 per cent. New lending rose 17 per cent to €12.3 billion, which included €3.2 billion of Irish mortgages, up 4 per cent.

AIB previously forecast customer loans would grow by around 5 per cent this year. In the trading update, the bank has raised its full-year 2026 forecast for customer loan growth to 5–6 per cent.

The bank has also raised its net interest income forecast to more than €3.85 billion, up from more than €3.8 billion previously.

It said the forecast was upgraded “based on rate assumptions” of a European Central Bank deposit rate of 2.5 per cent and a Bank of England rate of 4 per cent at December 2026.

Deposits held by customers have increased by 2.7 per cent to €120.4 billion, while AIB’s costs rose 3 per cent in the nine months and its cost-to-income ratio was 44 per cent.

The rise in costs, linked in part to salary inflation, was partially offset by lower average staff numbers, which fell 3 per cent year-on-year from 10,351 to 10,017 by the end of September 2026.

AIB chief executive Colin Hunt said the financial update showed the bank “had another strong quarter”, which reflected the resilience of the Irish economy.

“While the international environment remains uncertain, our disciplined approach, market-leading franchise and strong capital position enable us to continue to support our 3.5 million customers, the communities we serve and the wider Irish economy.

“As we enter the final months of our current strategic cycle, we remain focused on delivering sustainable growth and shareholder returns.”

He added that investors would be updated by the bank on its next strategic plan, up to 2030, in March 2027.

AIB has maintained its guidance on costs increasing by around 2 per cent this year and return on tangible equity of above 20 per cent, while other income is expected to be close to €800 million.

Last month, AIB announced a reduction of up to 0.35 per cent on its four-year fixed rate for mortgages over €250,000, with the reduction available to those whose homes don’t have a building energy rating of B3 or higher.

In October 2025, AIB also reduced a number of its non-green fixed mortgage rates by up to 0.65 per cent, which it estimated could benefit more than 10,000 people each month.

The bank’s latest financial update, which said AIB has a 28.4 per cent share of Ireland’s mortgage market, said green mortgages represented 61 per cent of new mortgage lending this year.

In March of this year, AIB announced a €1 billion share buyback programme. The bank said it completed €740 million of the buyback by the end of September and by November 3rd, the total had reached about €849 million.

]]><![CDATA[Operating profits at Convention Centre Dublin fall 21% to €6m]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/04/operating-profits-at-convention-centre-dublin-fall-21-to-6m/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/04/operating-profits-at-convention-centre-dublin-fall-21-to-6m/Wed, 04 Nov 2026 13:16:59 +0000Operating profits at the company that runs the Convention Centre Dublin (CCD) last year decreased by 21 per cent to €6.2 million despite attendance numbers rising to almost 150,000.

Accounts filed by Spencer Dock Convention Centre (SDCC) show that operating profits decreased as revenues declined by 10 per cent from €32.34 million to €29.22 million.

Next week, the CCD is due to host two large events connected to Ireland’s European Union (EU) presidency that includes an informal meeting of EU leaders on Friday, November 13th.

Some of the guest speakers to appear at CCD events in 2025 included former US politician Hillary Clinton, former tennis player Andre Agassi and former boxer Sugar Ray Leonard.

Income from events declined by almost 13 per cent to €21.9 million in 2025. Last year, the Convention Centre Dublin welcomed almost 150,000 people, who attended a total of 122 events.

This compares to more than 134,000 people attending a total of 114 events at CCD in 2024

SDCC received the remaining revenues of €7.29 million in unitary charge payments from the owner of the convention centre, the Office of Public Works (OPW). The payment is to cover the capital cost of building the centre.

The contract with the OPW includes performance criteria that must be met throughout the 25-year operational contract, which commenced in 2010.

Chief executive, Stephen Meehan said: “The Convention Centre Dublin had another strong operational performance last year.”

Meehan said that “trading at the CCD during this year has been positive. So far during 2026, the CCD has hosted a total of 98 events and welcomed over 205,000 attendees.”

The firm recorded pretax profits of €15.26 million last year due to net interest payments received of €8.28 million along with a €775,000 impairment reversal.

The company recorded a post tax profit of €13.82 million after incurring a corporation tax charge of €1.44 million.

In June 2023, UK infrastructure investor John Laing Group completed the acquisition of the operating licence and public-private partnership (PPP) for the CCD.

Last year, SDCC paid out dividends of €10.4m compared to €13.4 million in 2024.

While the total number of events increased during 2025, overall income from events declined due to a change in the mix of events year-on-year.

The income from an event will depend on the type, duration and size of the specific event in question. Accumulated profits totalled €27.2 million.

A related firm, Spencer Dock Centre Dublin (No 2) DAC employs the staff that operates the centre and last year numbers employed decreased by four to 77.

Staff costs increased marginally from €5.24 million to €5.36 million. Pay to directors decreased from €667,140 to €559,132.

]]><![CDATA[British Ambassador to Ireland Kara Owen on current Anglo-Irish relations, trade opportunities, and the possibility of a Brexit reversal]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/podcasts/inside-business/british-ambassador-to-ireland-kara-owen-on-current-anglo-irish-relations-trade-opportunities-and-the-possibility-of-a-brexit-reversal/https://www.irishtimes.com/podcasts/inside-business/british-ambassador-to-ireland-kara-owen-on-current-anglo-irish-relations-trade-opportunities-and-the-possibility-of-a-brexit-reversal/Wed, 04 Nov 2026 16:00:16 +0000On this week’s Inside Business host Ciarán Hancock is joined by Kara Owen, the British ambassador to Ireland.

She started in the role in October 2025, having had a long career in the British diplomatic service. Kara was previously British High Commissioner to Singapore from 2019 to 2024 and, before that, was Director for the Americas at the Foreign and Commonwealth Office.

Her diplomatic career has also included senior postings in Paris and Hanoi, as well as serving as Private Secretary to the Foreign Secretary.

In a wide-ranging interview, Kara covers her decision to visit all 26 counties in her first year in the role, the current state of Anglo-Irish relations, and talk of Britain rejoining the EU at some point.

]]>Dara Mac Dónaill<![CDATA[Glanbia revenue rises in first nine months of 2026]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/04/glanbia-revenue-rises-in-first-nine-months-of-2026/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/04/glanbia-revenue-rises-in-first-nine-months-of-2026/Wed, 04 Nov 2026 08:26:24 +0000Nutrition group Glanbia said on Wednesday that its revenue grew in the first nine months of the year as prices rose and volumes increased on the back of strong consumer trends in protein and energy categories.

The group also raised its guidance on full-year earnings-per-share growth.

Revenue growth in the first nine months was just under 10 per cent on a like-for-like basis. Volume growth was seen across Glanbia’s three business segments.

Revenues in its Performance Nutrition brand category rose 18 per cent, driven by an almost 14 per cent increase in prices and 4.3 per cent volume growth. In its Americas business, which accounts for 60 per cent of Performance Nutrition revenue for Glanbia, like-for-like revenue rose almost 12 per cent. Strong volumes and pricing growth in its international division drove revenue up almost 29 per cent.

Like-for-like revenue in Optimum Nutrition branded products grew almost 26 per cent on strong growth in the category, gains in market share and new distribution.

7-9: Since 1862, O’Connell’s pub has traded from Eyre Square. It remained in the O’Connell family until 2006, when Maureen O’Connell nominated St Vincent de Paul as the main beneficiary in her will. The dollar weakened against all significant peers, while the yield on 10-year Treasuries fell five basis points to 4.92 per cent. Europe’s Stoxx 600 rose 0.4 per cent while a gauge for Asian equities wavered.

Investors initially saw a Democratic wave as a potential setback for stocks given the prospect of tighter regulatory scrutiny, particularly of high-growth technology and artificial intelligence companies. Treasuries, meanwhile, stand to benefit if political gridlock limits further tax cuts and government spending, easing concerns about federal borrowing.

Democrats scored victories in Republican strongholds across the country, flipping at least seven Senate seats and winning House races in districts Republicans easily carried in 2024.

Several news organisations projected that Democrats would win the House, while Decision Desk HQ projected they took the Senate. Trump said he could work with a House and Senate run by the opposition “if the Democrats want to work with me.”

“Political gridlock should reduce the likelihood of another significant fiscal expansion, while the accompanying decline in Treasury yields could ultimately provide some support to equities,” said Florian Ielpo at Lombard Odier Investment Managers.

“The fundamental backdrop has not suddenly changed, with US growth remaining solid.”

“The US midterms, like any significant political event, have created uncertainty, widening the disconnect between market valuations and fundamentals,” said George Efstathopoulos, a money manager at Fidelity International.

“I am now trimming defensive positions, including utilities, to buy technology stocks in Asia and elsewhere, while adding some exposure to India for diversification.”

Bond investors have been uneasy about the US’s fiscal trajectory, with the nation’s debt load at around $40 trillion (€35.16 trillion), and gridlock may reduce the risk of additional spending or tax cuts that would require more Treasury issuance.

“Democratic control of Congress will make it harder for the White House administration to pass significant partisan legislation,” David Chao, a global market strategist at Invesco Asset Management, wrote in a note. “Less fiscal stimulus could reduce upward pressure on US growth, inflation and Treasury yields.”

In currency markets, the New Zealand dollar was the biggest gainer among significant markets versus the dollar, rising 0.7 per cent, while the yen and euro both strengthened 0.4 per cent.

“The US dollar’s Achilles’ heel is being exposed,” with its fortunes tied to the AI boom, said David Forrester, a senior strategist at Credit Agricole CIB in Singapore. “A Democrat blue wave that stifles data centre buildouts and hobbles the AI boom would weigh on the US dollar.”

Bitcoin slipped as much as 2.8 per cent on concerns that a Democratic sweep could stall industry-backed legislation and bring tougher scrutiny of digital-asset firms. The cryptocurrency later erased all of its declines.

Meanwhile, Oil fluctuated after a two-day decline as traders weighed mixed signals on the trajectory of US-Iran peace talks.

Brent traded near $104 a barrel after swinging in a range of more than $6 on Tuesday. West Texas Intermediate was around $97. Tehran and Washington are reviewing fresh proposals from mediators on how to resolve their differences, according to a diplomat briefed on the matter. Still, Iran’s national security chief said on X that the US response has so far been “not satisfactory.”

The latest diplomatic efforts follow weeks of heightened tensions, with Iran stepping up attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz and US President Donald Trump threatening renewed strikes after the midterms. Oil tumbled on Monday on signs of progress, but choppy trading returned Tuesday as deep divisions cast doubt on a breakthrough.

]]><![CDATA[Why buy expensive French tanks when what we need is cheap Irish drones?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/04/why-buy-expensive-french-tanks-when-what-we-need-is-cheap-irish-drones/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/04/why-buy-expensive-french-tanks-when-what-we-need-is-cheap-irish-drones/Wed, 04 Nov 2026 06:00:01 +0000The next time the Defence Forces’ plan to buy €1 billion worth of armoured vehicles from France comes up for discussion, somebody should really ask about Leopard tanks.

Arguably the best tank in the world, the German-made main battle tank was supposed to be a game changer when, after much hand-wringing, it was supplied to Ukraine in 2023 alongside similar behemoths: the British Challenger and the US Abrams. They were predicted to give Ukraine the upper hand over Russia on the battlefield.

They didn’t. What halted the advance of the Russian army and now enforces the stalemate on the battlefield is drones. Lots of them. Cheap and deadly. Made in Ukraine.

History is full of examples of unsuccessful generals who made the mistake of fighting the last war. Instead of adjusting to how the nature of conflict is being changed by technology, they just try to do what worked last time, only better. The Russians, who expected to roll over Ukraine in a couple of weeks based on their previous experience, are just the latest example.

Ireland should be careful not to fall into that trap. The Irish Army obviously needs vehicles but seems to have shaped its future role around turning itself into a conventional armoured brigade that can – don’t say it too loudly – fight alongside other European armies in the sort of battle groups that have been potentially rendered obsolete by the conflict in Ukraine.

The other task that is envisioned for the Army once it’s tooled up is deployment overseas on UN missions. There has not been a UN deployment authorised since 2011, and the mandate for Unifil – Ireland’s most significant deployment in Lebanon – is not being renewed when it runs out at the end of the year.

Not accepting the regrettable but real decline in the global role of the UN is also tantamount to fighting the last war.

The real elephant in the room is where are we going to find the soldiers to fight in these new tanks. The Defence Forces simply does not provide an attractive career for many. That might change. Driving tanks and going overseas are the sort of things that professional soldiers like doing.

Dangers on a train: Russia’s improved drones pose new threat to Ukrainian rail users

But the question that nobody seems to want to ask, however, is whether reshaping the Defence Forces around new armoured vehicles is really the most effective and economical way to defend our land and sea borders now that drones and missiles dominate the battlefield.

Paradoxically, the neglect of the Defence Forces over the years presents Ireland with a unique opportunity to skip a generation of military technology and create a force able to fulfil this goal at a cost that is realistic. And one that could attract the best and brightest engineering and technological talent.

‘Whatever Trump and Putin agree, we’ll fight the invaders’: Inside the dugouts powering Ukraine’s drone war

Our complete lack of a domestic arms industry means that, unlike our larger European partners, we are not trapped by history. Big countries end up locked into feeding their arms manufacturers in what former US president and D-Day commander Dwight Eisenhower dubbed the military-industrial complex.

This includes the French and hence their enthusiasm for selling us tanks. The cost will be enormous. As well as the upfront price, put at about €1 billion, we will be tied into a long-tailed maintenance contract with the French suppliers, which could bring the costs to many multiples of this.

Belgium bought 442 similar vehicles for €1.6 billion, but the lifetime cost is put at €14 billion, or €3.6 million per vehicle. It’s a lot of money for something that could be knocked out by a drone costing a couple of hundred euro.

The potential for marine drones to help police the 880,000sq km of seabed under Ireland’s jurisdiction, including vital submarine cables, is equally obvious for a Naval Service that faces real difficulties crewing its ships.

What adds to the paradox is that we already have a nascent drone industry, but seem determined to stamp it out. Manna Aero, the best-known Irish drone-maker, has abandoned attempts to set up a drone-based delivery service here, citing the lack of a national drone strategy. This was after it was refused planning permission by Dún Laoghaire-Rathdown County Council for a drone delivery hub.

The main issue was concern over the intrusive nature of drones, which will remain a significant issue for drone deliveries in urban areas. Not so much on battlefields.

Manna is a relatively small player, but its technological abilities are well regarded. It is not in the military drone space and has expressed no interest in the area publicly. The question as to whether Ireland’s security would be better served by investing €14 billion into making our own air and sea drones is one well worth asking before signing a cheque for new tanks.

If the reader’s role was “truly redundant”, this would indicate a “very disorganised” employer, says Michelle Halloran, independent HR consultant and workplace investigator of Halloran HR Resolutions.

“It seems quite odd; it’s a very peculiar decision after only three months that a role is redundant. That sounds very strange to me.

“At best, it doesn’t sound very well organised and doesn’t demonstrate a lot of foresight on the part of the employer,” she says.

While it could have been “sloppy planning”, it might be more justifiable if the company suddenly lost an account or client, and the timing was “just really bad luck” for the reader, she says.

By the 1880s, supercharged by the rapid spread of office work, the typewriter and shorthand – the 2,000-year-old technique of using written symbols to speed the recording and transcription of speech – had combined to create new job opportunities for many women.

Before office work expanded in the US and Europe, social norms confined most of them to traditional “female roles” such as teaching or domestic service. But shorthand and especially typing were marketed as particularly suited to the female mentality and physique. By 1900, three-quarters of shorthand typists in the US were women – hence the distress of male clerks. Their protests were in vain. By 1930, 95 per cent of the US profession were women.

Yet shorthand and typing were a double-edged sword. Given a chance to enter the workforce, some women thrived. For instance, many British suffragists and suffragettes were expert typists who used their office skills as levers of emancipation, for instance, to prepare, print and distribute leaflets.

Secretarial skills also helped the first women stockbrokers, journalists and publishers break into their professions. Others enjoyed secretarial work simply for the flexibility and cash it provided to develop other career paths.

But many shorthand typists were consigned to life under a very low glass ceiling, far removed from the rosy imaginings of the late 19th century’s women pioneers. The determination and sacrifices required to progress in full-time paid work were sometimes too great.

The second lesson is that the intervention of aggressive consultants, selling technology on grounds of efficiency, is often bad for the people at the sharp end of that implementation.

By the 1910s, “scientific managers”, inspired by consultant Frederick Winslow Taylor’s mechanistic push to make manufacturing more efficient, were putting speedometers on typewriters to assess productivity. One Taylor disciple, William Henry Leffingwell, author of 1917’s Scientific Office Management, obsessed over the best way secretaries should arrange a desk (“keeping stationery in desk drawers is [a] source of waste motion”), how long it should take to insert a sheet of paper in a typewriter (three one-hundredths of a minute), and whether it paid to take paper clips off correspondence before filing (it depends: it takes 10 minutes to remove one pound of clips, he calculated).

Leffingwell was naturally a big advocate of the typing pool, which grouped shorthand typists together rather than relying on “small groups of uncontrolled stenographers throughout the office who work only part of their time on letters and part on miscellaneous clerical tasks and, as is often the case, sit in absolute idleness at other times”.

Historian Lucienne Boyce, who worked as a temporary secretary in the 1970s, says: “The whole image of the typing pool was of a factory, and the women became instruments ... just as you keep workers down in a factory, by giving them a tiny bit of job to do.” Boyce later became a careers adviser and saw how rarely men were directed down the secretarial path.

This was a world where “bosses, almost always male, literally dictate to female clericals”, as academic Catherine Rankovic has put it. As the century progressed, the combination of complete control, a rigid focus on efficiency, and lower status sucked from the office what little autonomy and joy women had hoped they might achieve there. It created what sociologist Margery Davies called a “secretarial proletariat”.

Obstacles that stood in the way of these women included formal or informal marriage bars, inadequate or non-existent maternity leave or childcare options, and looming disparities between the pay and promotion opportunities offered to women, not to mention casual sexism and outright sexual harassment.

A third lesson is that the same forces that lead to the birth of one technology can also hasten its demise at the hands of the next wave of development. The earlier technology’s users are often the unwitting victims. The Dictaphone, the electric typewriter, the computer and the internet finally put paid to the typing pool and consigned shorthand dictation to the shredder of secretarial skills.

With the advent of the desktop personal computer, the typewriter became a “keyboard” and the association of typing with women’s work broke down. Executives started to realise the quickest route from the idea in their heads to the memo or letter was through their own fingertips. “Now computers have come along, and ‘typing’ is ‘keyboarding’. Suddenly, voila! Men can type,” Gloria Steinem, the feminist activist, said in a 2007 commencement address at her alma mater Smith College. “Gives you faith in men’s ability to change, doesn’t it?”

So the dream that many women nursed in the late 19th century – that innovations such as shorthand and typing would provide a route into the workplace and a launch platform for promotion – was, for many, a hollow one. Only in the 2020s did women managers start to outnumber secretaries in the list of most common roles for women in the US.

But there is a fourth, and more upbeat, lesson from the rise and fall of the secretarial proletariat. New technologies can create opportunities for a smaller number of workers to cultivate skills that enable them to shape better jobs for themselves.

Secretaries have morphed into high-value personal and executive assistants, for instance, increasingly sought after for their command of the newest office tools.

Rebecca Siciliano, managing director of agency Tiger Recruitment, says a lot of her clients “want someone [who] is AI and tech savvy”.

These assistants must provide the expert human touch needed to juggle diaries packed with virtual and in-person meetings, and to represent their boss inside and outside the business. They need to know when to delegate to bots the more mundane tasks of taking minutes or updating spreadsheets. The best command salaries of £85,000 annually, according to Siciliano. Some may rise to become chiefs of staff and operations managers.

Much has changed since Pierson made the case for women in the workplace. The manual typewriter is long gone in most offices. The smartphone and AI are eradicating the last remnants of need for written shorthand. And despite Tiger and its clients’ best efforts to broaden the pool of executive assistants, only a small minority are men.

And why Trump and his Republican Party look set for a shellacking in today’s midterm elections.

Losing control of the House of Representatives appears to be a certainty. The question is whether the Democrats can also win the Senate.

This could hobble Trump’s presidency as Democrats would be in a position to block cabinet and judicial appointments while having subpoena powers to investigate the administration.

Even with the tariffs, US inflation would probably have slowed again this year if Trump hadn’t gone to war with Iran, triggering a spike in oil prices.

Trump’s own goal in the Middle East looks increasingly likely to define his presidency. It has not just driven up fuel prices but also the cost of diesel, which is needed to transport goods.

And reports suggest the US may be considering another strike on Iran, a move that is certain to fan another upward shift in energy prices.

The full ramifications of Trump’s war can be seen through the prism of US producer price inflation, which has surged above 6 per cent. This will translate into further consumer price inflation in the coming months.

How Trump reacts to a possible mauling in the midterms is difficult to forecast. Some commentators believe he will defy the traditional lame duck status it normally bestows on the White House incumbent because he’s Donald Trump and because he’s on the way out anyway.

But the era of executive orders and bypassing Congress might soon be at an end.

The top Democrat on the House oversight committee, Robert Garcia of California, says he will prioritise the examination of Trump’s family businesses, the Epstein files, immigration enforcement, corporate profiteering, and how US health secretary Robert Kennedy jnr has handled vaccines.

His final two years in office could yet prove to be explosive.

]]><![CDATA[How can my son find out if his father has cut him out of his will?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/03/how-can-my-son-find-out-if-his-father-has-cut-him-out-of-his-will/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/03/how-can-my-son-find-out-if-his-father-has-cut-him-out-of-his-will/Tue, 03 Nov 2026 06:00:01 +0000My son’s father and I never married. He has never paid maintenance for him. A few years ago there was a disagreement between them and unfortunately his father hasn’t had any contact with him for about five years.

My ex also has another son who he is very close to. Recently my ex came into some money from the sale of his own father’s house. In the event that he dies, how can our son find out if he left a will?

CC

In an ideal world, we all take care of family, not least when we die, assuming we have the resources to do so. The real world is more messy.

You don’t say whether your former partner was ever a part of your son’s life but he certainly never paid anything to the cost of raising him.

Now middle-aged, your son and his father no longer talk. Meanwhile, his father has a son from a separate relationship to whom he is close, and the father has come into money.

That certainly raises the potential for a dispute when he dies.

There are two scenarios here – one where he has a will and one where he does not. Let’s take them in reverse order.

If there is no will, his estate would be divided according to the Succession Act.

You do not say whether the father ever married – either to the mother of his other son or someone else. If he did, and presuming that spouse survives him, she will receive two-thirds of his estate with his children sharing the final third.

That would include your son, this favoured other son and any other children he might have.

If the spouse does not survive him, or there never was any spouse, the children split the value of the estate between them without regard to favourites. Everything is split evenly.

Whomever applies for the grant of administration intestate is obliged to track down all qualifying beneficiaries – which includes all children regardless of whether they were born inside or outside a marriage. In practice, whomever applies to manage the estate will engage a solicitor as intestacy can be a minefield.

But what if there is a will?

If it is like most other Irish wills and there is a spouse, it will simply leave everything to the spouse. If he does not, the spouse is entitled to what is called a legal right share – which, where there are children, amounts to one-third of the estate.

Assuming any legal right share is respected, the will could make provision for one or other or both sons – and any other children – but it doesn’t have to. There is no obligation for a person to provide in death for adult children or any other relative apart from a spouse.

However, if a child feels that they should be entitled to something in a will, they can take what is called a section 117 action.

Section 117 (1) of the Succession Act 1965 says: “Where, on application by or on behalf of a child of a testator, the court is of opinion that the testator has failed in his moral duty to make proper provision for the child in accordance with his means, whether by his will or otherwise, the court may order that such provision shall be made for the child out of the estate as the court thinks just.”

This is a very wide and nebulous position, with the court taking into account the circumstances of the applicant vis-à-vis other family members among other things.

It clarifies in section 117 (2): “The court shall consider the application from the point of view of a prudent and just parent, taking into account the position of each of the children of the testator and any other circumstances which the court may consider of assistance in arriving at a decision that will be as fair as possible to the child to whom the application relates and to the other children.”

The key thing is that any section 117 application must be made to the court within six months of a grant of probate.

And how do you know probate has been granted? In a harmonious family situation, you’d expect to be notified of this but in the scenario you outline, it may be a case of your son keeping tabs on the Probate Register where all grants of probate and grants on administration (in case of intestacy) are recorded – along with copies of the related will where one exists.

He will need his father’s first and surname and the year in which he died.

When will probate be granted? That depends on how efficiently whoever is managing the estate sort the paperwork and how complex the estate is. It generally takes a year or close to it anyway.

Is it worth pursuing a section 117? That depends on your son’s position in life and also what his father’s estate comprises. There is certainly no guarantee of success and there will be legal fees to consider.

Of course, there is nothing to say that this money your ex has recently come into will still be part of his estate when he dies. It could well have been dissipated by then – either because it was spent or because it was gifted to other family members.

The Section 117 procedure only refers to provision in a will or lack thereof. It does not cover lifetime gifts.

]]><![CDATA[State requires large number of workers from outside European Economic Area, according to ESRI ]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/11/03/state-still-needs-large-numbers-of-workers-from-outside-european-economic-area/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/11/03/state-still-needs-large-numbers-of-workers-from-outside-european-economic-area/Tue, 03 Nov 2026 06:00:01 +0000Ireland continues to require large numbers of workers from non-European Economic Area (EAA) countries to address labour shortages, but it struggles to retain many of them, according to Economic and Social Research Institute research.

Its report found the number of non-EEA workers – those from outside the EU, Norway, Iceland or Liechtenstein – that were recruited increased substantially between 2021 and 2025 in all but one of 25 sectors.

The exception was the information and communications technology (ICT) sector, where the number fell 21 per cent, the report to be published on Tuesday said.

Despite the continuing need to recruit high-skilled worked in other areas, especially healthcare, the number of General Employment Permits (GEPs) issued to lower or mid-skill level workers had exceeded, in 2024, the number of Critical Skills Permits (CSPs) going to those with the most urgently needed qualifications or experience. This was the first time this had happened in almost a decade.

The number of CSP holders leaving again after coming to Ireland to work is also substantially higher than those with GEPs with 40 per cent versus 21 per cent after two years and 60 per cent versus 50 per cent after five years.

Citing Department of Justice figures, the research suggests the figures for those with graduate-level education are significantly lower.

The growth in the number of permits issued between 2021 and 2025 was skewed by the Covid pandemic with many migrant workers leaving during that time and many coming here to fill vacancies as workplaces opened up again in its aftermath.

There have also been a number of changes to the regulations during the period with the easing of restrictions on what roles overseas workers could be granted a GEP to fill and, more recently, a review of the circumstances in which the 50:50 rule might be waived. This rule requires that a majority of workers in a workplace be EEA citizens.

The number of companies recruiting from outside the EEA, meanwhile, has steadily grown to 8,328 in 2025. Just 20 of those firms accounted for about 10 per cent of the total of more than 31,000 permits. Google topped a list that included other tech firms as well as some operating in the professional services and health sectors.

However, the majority – 4,740 – only applied for one permit to fill a vacancy.

The number of non-EEA students entitled to work some hours in Ireland to help support themselves topped 56,000, almost double the figure for 2021, with Brazilians making up more than a quarter of the total on 15,077.

“The strong uptake in employment permits shows the growing importance of non-EEA migrant workers in meeting Ireland’s demand for labour across healthcare, construction and ICT services,” said Ada Sophia Hahn, who wrote the report with Dervla Potter.

“Ensuring that the employment permit system is effective and fair matters not only to employers and migrant workers but also to Irish society at large as it could impact the delivery of public services.

“Consistently low retention services would be a concern, as it could undermine the effectiveness of the system.”

Members of the migrant worker community are due to protest outside the Dáil on Tuesday over proposed changes to Ireland’s citizenship requirements.

]]>Robert Kirk<![CDATA[Opinion polls are core to how media covers politics, but is that a good thing?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/media/2026/11/03/opinion-polls-are-core-to-how-media-covers-politics-but-is-that-a-good-thing/https://www.irishtimes.com/media/2026/11/03/opinion-polls-are-core-to-how-media-covers-politics-but-is-that-a-good-thing/Tue, 03 Nov 2026 06:00:00 +0000On Tuesday, Americans vote in midterm elections with consequences for everyone around the world. As usual, much of the campaign coverage has revolved around opinion polls, which give the Democrats a national lead of up to 11 points on the generic congressional ballot, while the party’s candidates are challenging for Senate seats in places where they usually wouldn’t have a hope.

Despite all that polling data, many remain sceptical about whether these predictions will be proved correct. Regardless, polls have been central to the coverage, as they are in most elections.

Polling has been a fixture of political journalism for almost 90 years. Its modern form dates from 1936, when George Gallup used a small but carefully chosen sample to predict Franklin Roosevelt’s landslide, humiliating the Literary Digest, whose vast survey of its own affluent readers had backed his opponent. Gallup’s results were syndicated to newspapers across the country, beginning a partnership between pollsters and the press that has lasted ever since.

But it was not until the 1970s, or in Ireland’s case the 1980s, that newspapers began to invest seriously in polls of their own. The Market Research Bureau of Ireland, founded by Jack Jones in 1962, spent years researching washing powder and air travel before turning to politics, and the Irish Times/MRBI series that began in the early 1980s became the benchmark here.

There has been no shortage of criticism of the relationship. Newspapers, it is suggested, over-dramatise results, splashing shouty headlines about tiny shifts that are within the margin of error. Polling is also blamed for “horse race” coverage that treats elections as sporting fixtures, ignoring the issues at stake. One Harvard study of the 2016 US presidential race found policy accounted for just a tenth of coverage, less than a quarter of the space devoted to who was ahead.

These criticisms are not without foundation, although research across 27 European countries suggests poll-driven coverage is most common in tight, multiparty contests, where knowing the state of play can help voters decide how to use their ballots.

Distrust of the polls themselves has also grown, with people pointing to glaring misses such as Brexit or Donald Trump’s first victory. That has been compounded by the rise of populist movements whose supporters are often underrepresented in surveys, prompting accusations of bias. Despite all this, a study of more than 200 elections in 32 countries found no evidence that polling errors were increasing.

Three elections in the past 10 days have highlighted some of these issues. In Brazil, the final surveys had incumbent president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva ahead in the first round, which his opponent Flávio Bolsonaro edged, then gave Bolsonaro a narrow lead in the runoff, which Lula won by more than three points. Neither error was particularly large, but each picked the wrong winner.

In Israel, the final polls correctly predicted deadlock but underestimated both Likud and the Arab parties.

And in Serbia, where public polling is sparse and voters had reason to be wary of declaring opposition sympathies, surveys showing Aleksandar Vucic’s party narrowly ahead were proved completely wrong when the student-led opposition won an outright majority.

The Irish Times view on Serbia’s election: youthquake in Belgrade

Traditional polling is being reshaped by changes in the media industry. Falling revenues have made publishers less enthusiastic about the expensive business of high-quality polling. That has led to a move from face-to-face interviewing towards cheaper online panels, weighted to reflect the profile of the electorate.

In Ireland, Red C for the Business Post and Ireland Thinks for the Sunday Independent now alternate monthly online surveys, while The Irish Times’s face-to-face poll with Ipsos B&A appears several times a year. The methods can return somewhat different results. Red C, for example, regularly puts Fianna Fáil a few points lower than other pollsters do. But overall performance has been respectable, with final polls in 2024 largely within the margin of error. Every poll is a snapshot in time, and across volatile referendum campaigns, surveys and results have often diverged wildly.

The field has narrowed too, with titles such as the Sunday Times Irish edition no longer commissioning polls.

Elsewhere, there are signs of questionable standards. In September, an undercover investigation by Channel 4 News and the Verbatim group revealed that polls carried prominently by the Times and the Telegraph had been arranged by Reform UK figures and paid for through what they believed was an American donor’s company, without either paper being told.

In the US, a firm called Wedgewood Polls admitted last week that it had fabricated results reported by The New York Times, Newsweek and others. One Michigan Democratic candidate says a fake survey showing her in single digits drove away her donors and ended her Senate campaign.

The problem in both cases lay with news organisations failing to verify where the numbers came from and what financial incentives might have been involved. But what is even worse is that some US outlets are giving prominence to the almost completely unregulated prediction markets that have mushroomed in recent years. CNN and CNBC have partnerships with Kalshi, and Wall Street Journal owner Dow Jones with Polymarket, on undisclosed terms.

This seems a highly dubious proposition, since betting odds can be moved by anyone with deep enough pockets. The old model, in which media organisations paid for polls and stood over the results, may have had its flaws but this particular replacement looks considerably worse.

]]><![CDATA[Don’t make an additional voluntary contribution to your pension – until you read this]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/03/dont-make-an-additional-voluntary-contribution-to-your-pension-until-you-read-this/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/03/dont-make-an-additional-voluntary-contribution-to-your-pension-until-you-read-this/Tue, 03 Nov 2026 05:55:00 +0000Retirement savers have just another two weeks or so until the November 18th deadline for tax relief on additional voluntary contributions (AVCs) for 2025 passes.

Often described as “turbo fuel” for your pension, the benefits of these payments are many. You can maximise available tax relief, improve your chances of retiring early, and you’ll hopefully have a bigger fund to draw down in retirement thanks to them.

But before you lock your money away through AVCs, it’s also worth taking a moment to consider if they are the best option for your money at a particular point in time.

Your money is locked away

Once you put additional money into your pension, it is locked away until you can retire. But what if you need it for your health? Your children? To pay down expensive debts? Repairs on your house, or just for those holidays you want to take now, rather than wait until retirement?

“It’s really a case of having a financial plan – and prioritising what’s most important,” says Mark Ryan, director of My Wealth Management.

Putting money into the stock market, an investment fund, or a high-yielding deposit account can still give you the potential for real gains, while maintaining flexibility. Of course, you are giving up on the tax relief – but this might be okay.

“Tax relief, while it’s great, shouldn’t be the only consideration. It’s of little benefit if it leaves you short of money for other needs,” says Sinead McEvoy, head of retirement solutions at Standard Life.

For McEvoy, a solid approach can be doing “a bit of both”. Put some money into a rainy-day fund, for example, and some into an AVC.

She is often asked whether or not you should prioritise your pension, or paying your mortgage.

Managing your money and your time in retirement

For some, the psychological impact of paying off a mortgage is huge, and this can take priority when it comes to spare cash. But focusing on it solely may not be the right approach either.

“I don’t think I’d pay off all your mortgage and ignore your pension,” she says. “Think of all the compounding you’re missing out on by paying off your mortgage.”

“It would be a preference for some people,” Ryan agrees, referring to paying down the mortgage first. Another option, he suggests, is to boost your AVCs now, and hope for investment growth, and use the bigger lump sum when you retire to pay down the mortgage at that point.

You won’t benefit from the same tax relief as AVCs by paying down your mortgage, so it can be worthwhile to “crunch the numbers” before making a decision.

Indeed, there can be an opportunity cost of this approach; you are giving up on tax relief, which can supercharge your pension fund.

Consider €200 invested every month for 10 years. If it returns an average of 6 per cent a year, it will deliver almost €32,500. But if tax relief had been available, at the higher rate, you would have had €280 going into the investment each month – so the return would have been significantly higher, at €45,500. You just wouldn’t have been able to withdraw it.

You may end up paying a higher tax rate in retirement

“I get asked this question often,” says Ryan. “Why would I put in money to get tax relief at 40 per cent when I pay it at the same rate in retirement?”

Remember, the tax relief you enjoy on AVCs is only deferred; when you draw down your pension, you may pay income tax on it. So then, you need to bear in mind the value of this tax relief – while it will grow tax-free, which is very beneficial, it can be particularly valuable if you get relief on it today as a higher rate taxpayer, and draw it down at the standard rate of tax in retirement.

While a higher tax rate in retirement is indicative of a healthy fund, it may be a consideration for those close to the higher tax bracket.

“Those on the borderline (of the higher rate), and considering AVCs, then it’s a conversation worth having,” says Ryan. “I have had scenarios where people have decided not to do AVCs because of that.”

Others, however, will opt for the ‘bird in the hand’ approach, and take what’s on offer now – tax relief – rather than predict how the future might play out.

This decision may be only for a certain cohort, however. First of all, to maximise your tax-free lump sum on retirement of €200,000, you will need a fund of €800,000 – 25 per cent is tax-free; amounts between €200,000 and €500,000 are taxed at 20 per cent. “And that’s a significant pension fund for most,” says McEvoy. “Typically, people are underfunding their pensions.”

Lessons for a happy retirement from a year interviewing Ireland’s top leaders

So, paying in AVCs can help bump up your tax-free lump sum.

And, paying tax at the higher rate on your pension “just isn’t the case for most people” says McEvoy, pointing to the more generous tax bands available for the over-65s.

As our table shows, a married couple with an annual pension income of €36,126 won’t pay any tax in retirement, while single people aged 65 and over won’t pay tax on earnings of less than €18,000.

However, as income rises, retirees will see a growing proportion of their income taxed at the higher rate. A single person earning €45,563 from a combination of state pension and private pension income, for example, will pay a certain portion of their income at the higher rate of 40 per cent (€1,563 for 2026), thus pushing their effective rate up to 12.3 per cent. And it increases from there; someone earning €75,563 a year in retirement will pay the top rate of tax on €31, 563 of their income – for an effective tax rate of 24.5 per cent.

AVCs have to be drawn down at the same time as an occupational pension

Having different pension vehicles in play may give you greater flexibility as to when you have to draw down your pension. PRSAs (Personal Retirement Savings Accounts), for example, can be drawn down between 60 – or 50 if it isn’t tied to an employment – and 75. It might also help keep your pension income in retirement taxed at the lower rate.

Remember, however AVCs are funded – either through the main scheme or an AVC PRSA – they are tied to this main scheme.

“When you have an AVC, it must be retired at the same time as the main scheme,” says McEvoy. So, there is no flexibility available when putting your AVC money into a separate pension vehicle.

However, there might be the opportunity to segment your pension into different PRSAs at retirement, so that you can draw them down at different ages.

There is some flexibility, however, if you’re not happy with the fund choices offered in your occupational/public sector scheme.

AVC PRSAs can be used to offer greater investment choice. But the charges might be higher than in your occupational scheme, so this should be considered.

What are AVCs?

In short, AVCs are additional payments you make to your occupational or public sector pension to boost your fund, and hopefully your income in retirement.

If you have already maximised your matching contributions (ie, your employer contributes 6 per cent of salary if you contribute 6 per cent), and you have extra cash, you can consider putting this into your pension via an AVC.

As with all pension savings, the big advantage here is the tax relief you get – if you’re a higher rate taxpayer, for example, a €1,000 contribution to your pension will only cost you €600.

How much you can contribute and avail of tax relief will depend on Revenue limits. Tax relief is offered as a percentage of your net earnings, and increases in line with your age. So, if you’re aged between 30 and 39, for example, you can put 20 per cent of your earnings into your pension and get tax relief on it (so up to €10,000 a year if you earn €50,000, for example). This percentage increases to 30 per cent for those aged 50-54; 35 per cent for 55-59; and 40 per cent for 60 and over.

When it comes to making an AVC, you can do so on a regular or one-off basis, so they offer good flexibility. A maximum annual limit of €115,000 applies.

If you haven’t made AVCs for 2025, and you do so before the online tax return deadline of November 18th, you will be due a tax saving.

]]><![CDATA[Could Ireland’s Philip Lane be in the running for top ECB post? ]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/03/could-irelands-philip-lane-be-in-the-running-for-top-ecb-post/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/03/could-irelands-philip-lane-be-in-the-running-for-top-ecb-post/Tue, 03 Nov 2026 05:05:00 +0000The top job in the European Central Bank (ECB) is up for grabs following Christine Lagarde’s decision to step down early.

It sets off an intense period of haggling among euro zone states, with two other jobs also to be filled on the ECB board – those of the Republic’s Philip Lane, who is chief economist, and Isabel Schnabel, a German board member.

In this context, the comment by Central Bank of Ireland governor Gabriel Makhlouf that Lane would be a “great” candidate to be the next ECB president is interesting. Odds on the Irish man would be long, with Dutch and Spanish central bank governors Klaas Knot and Pablo Hernández de Cos seen as the front-runners.

Makhlouf says Philip Lane would be ‘great’ candidate to succeed Lagarde

But Makhlouf’s comments suggest two things. One is that while the Dutch and Spanish bankers are the current favourites, there is a long way to go in this race. In particular, it remains to be seen whether the euro zone governments who make the choice want to appoint a traditional central banker, or want to go – as they did the last time – for someone with a political background.

Makhlouf appears to believe that the Republic should take an active approach to the appointment, rather than just supporting one of the two current front-runners. In the haggling that follows, this could allow other Irish people to be put forward for other senior jobs on offer either in the ECB or other EU institutions.

While ECB rules limit executive board membership to one eight-year term, sources suggest that based on a previous contest, this does not apply if someone is stepping up to be president or vice-president. In any event, Lane still looks like an outsider at the moment, albeit eminently qualified and experienced.

The ECB presidency appointment will be driven by the large member states and comes at a time when wobbles in the bond market, particularly relating to France, mean the job will be a politically delicate one. With German chancellor Friedrich Merz looking over his shoulder at the AfD opposition party, which opposes ECB help for debtor countries, French president Emmanuel Macron in a weak domestic position and Spain heading for a general election, anything could happen.

<item rdf:about="https://orf.at/stories/3447232/">
   <title>Kein Regierungspersonal für Parteikanäle</title>
   <description>Der Verfassungsgerichtshof (VfGH) hat am Mittwoch eine Regelung zur Betreuung von Social-Media-Accounts von Regierungsmitgliedern aufgehoben. Die 2025 eingeführte Regel hatte es ermöglicht, dass Medienkanäle von Politikerinnen und Politikern bzw. von Parteien oder parteinahen Organisationen durch Kabinettsmitarbeiterinnen und -mitarbeiter betreut werden konnten.</description>
