Polish political leaders have reacted to the results of Tuesday’s US midterm elections, in which the Democrats won control of both houses of Congress from President Donald Trump’s Republicans.

The outcome was welcomed by Poland’s ruling coalition, with Prime Minister Donald Tusk declaring that “democracy won”. The response was more muted from the right-wing opposition and the office of conservative President Karol Nawrocki, who is a Trump ally.

🚨 🇺🇸 Tusk gives Trump some great advice. But will the US president listen?

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk urged the US president to seek compromises after the Republicans' defeat and not to rely on vetoes as his main way of governing.

Trump had earlier threatened to become… pic.twitter.com/s3E6G5zIQT

— NEXTA (@nexta_tv) November 4, 2026

Tusk addressed the election results on Wednesday afternoon local time at a press conference alongside his Czech counterpart, Andrej Babiš. “Today, democracy won in America,” said a smiling Tusk. “I love democracy; it is a beautiful thing.”

“As President Donald Trump himself said just after the election, the Democrats did a good job, and I really could not agree more with him this time,” added Tusk. “I hope that the result will stabilise the situation also in our region.”

Although the United States remains Poland’s most important security partner, Tusk’s government – a broad, pro-EU coalition that ranges from left to centre right – has at times had uneasy relations with the Trump administration.

It has been critical of Trump’s conciliatory approach towards Russia, his often tough stance on Ukraine, as well as his pursuit of US control over Greenland.

 

Meanwhile, the head of the parliamentary caucus of Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) party, Zbigniew Konwiński, told broadcaster Polsat News that “personally, I was happy with the Democrats’ victory”.

“We know how Donald Trump behaves, how volatile he is in his political declarations, how he can sometimes put Ukraine in a more difficult position than Russia, so I would rather look for the positives in what happened,” said Konwiński.

“If we look at recent years, the more Democrats, the stronger the Democrats, the better for Poland,” he added.

.@Konwinski_PO: Cieszę się z wygranej Demokratów w USA, bo to lepszy scenariusz dla Polski. @marcinfijolek pic.twitter.com/gJ3TnlMn0l

— Graffiti_PN (@Graffiti_PN) November 4, 2026

The speaker of Poland’s parliament, Włodzimierz Czarzasty, who is also the leader of one of KO’s junior coalition partners, The Left (Lewica), has clashed with the US ambassador to Poland twice this year over Czarzasty’s criticism of Trump.

Today, Czarzasty shared and commented on a social media post by Trump, published in the wake of the Democrats’ victory, in which the US president showed an image of his signature red cap with the word “VETO” on it.

“Where have I heard this before?” wrote Czarzasty, referring to the fact that Nawrocki has vetoed a record number of bills passed by parliament, where Tusk’s coalition has a majority.

Czarzasty then went on to list a series of characteristics that he suggested both Trump and Nawrocki share, including “arrogance”, “lack of respect for women”, a “suspicious past”, “transactional exploitation of their position”, and “admiration for politicians with fascist tendencies”.

Skąd ja to znam? Arogancja. Buta. Nieuzasadniona pewność siebie. Brak szacunku dla kobiet ( a to popchnę jakąś dwojga nazwisk, a to zakpię prymitywnie). Dziwna przeszłość. Instrumentalne traktowanie dziennikarzy. Pieniądze za spotkania. Transakcyjne wykorzystywanie funkcji.… pic.twitter.com/ryT2BMOZb2

— Włodzimierz Czarzasty 📚📖 (@wlodekczarzasty) November 4, 2026

Nawrocki has closely aligned himself with Trump. During last year’s Polish presidential election campaign, Trump invited Nawrocki for a private meeting at the White House. His then-homeland security secretary, Kristi Noem, visited Poland to endorse Nawrocki.

Nawrocki himself has not thus far commented on Tuesday’s midterm election results. However, Marcin Przydacz, the head of the president’s International Policy Bureau, did address the issue in a social media post.

“As predicted, in the US midterm elections voters decided on change,” wrote Przydacz. “Poland will continue its good cooperation with the US, because it is our ally, and collaboration is in our mutual interest.”

Przydacz also added that the results were “a reminder for Tusk” that “no government lasts forever”. In Poland, too, “the moment will come when voters will decide on change – and it might be quite soon”, added Przydacz, in a nod to next year’s Polish parliamentary elections.

Zgodnie z przewidywaniami w wyborach połówkowych w USA wyborcy zdecydowali o zmianie. Wcześniej wygrywali Republikanie, dziś Demokraci. Polska będzie kontynuować dobrą współpracę z USA, bo jest to nasz sojusznik, a kooperacja jest w naszym wspólnym interesie. O tym, kto sprawuje…

— Marcin Przydacz (@marcin_przydacz) November 4, 2026

Tusk’s foreign minister, Radosław Sikorski, meanwhile, used the US election results to revive his long-running feud with Elon Musk, who is no longer part of the Trump administration but donated enormous amounts of money to support the Republicans agead of the midterms.

Last year, Musk and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio criticised Sikorski after he suggested that Musk had threatened Ukraine. In a post on his social media platform, X, Musk told Sikorski to “be quiet, small man”.

On Wednesday, Tusk shared a screenshot of a tweet he had published last year, after Musk left the Trump administration, in which Sikorski wrote: “See, big man, politics is harder than you thought.”

pic.twitter.com/r6h2B5WfWa

— Radosław Sikorski 🇵🇱🇪🇺 (@sikorskiradek) November 4, 2026

]]> International Commission of Jurists criticises takeover of Polish constitutional court https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/11/04/international-commission-of-jurists-criticises-takeover-of-polish-constitutional-court/ Wed, 04 Nov 2026 11:05:52 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=106374

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!

Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.

The International Commission of Jurists (ICJ) has criticised the takeover of Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) by a group of government-backed judges. It says that the move “contravenes international standards on the independence of the judiciary”.

However, the ICJ, a Swiss-based NGO led by judges, lawyers and academics from around the world, also chastised Poland’s opposition-aligned president, Karol Nawrocki, for his role in the crisis around the TK, in particular his refusal to swear in judges elected by parliament.

🚨#Poland’s constitutional crisis must be resolved through the rule of law. The ICJ urges all authorities to respect judicial independence, follow lawful procedures, and comply with European court rulings.

🔗More information: https://t.co/NWmca9mpUx

— ICJ (@ICJ_org) November 3, 2026

On Friday, eight judges who were elected to the TK this year by the government’s parliamentary majority effectively took over the tribunal. They announced that the chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, and his deputy, Bartłomiej Sochański, had been suspended for failing to properly fulfil their duties.

Meanwhile, large numbers of riot police were deployed outside the court, holding back protesters, including opposition politicians, and preventing Święczkowski and Sochański from entering the grounds.

Święczkowski denounced the takeover of the court as an illegal “coup d’état”. He has been backed by the tribunal’s remaining six judges, who, like him, were appointed under the rule of the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, which brought the TK under its political influence.

Nawrocki, who is also aligned with PiS, has likewise denounced the actions of the government-backed judges. In the early hours of Saturday, he dramatically forced his way into the court, where he clashed physically and verbally with the judges who had taken over the TK.

During a visit to the Constitutional Tribunal last night, President Nawrocki clashed physically and verbally with judges involved in an attempt to take control of the court.

The president is today seeking talks with political leaders to discuss the crisis https://t.co/7HmBnuIaDG

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 31, 2026

In a statement on Tuesday, the ICJ expressed regret that the latest developments have “deepened the crisis over the tribunal”. It called on Polish “state institutions to seek solutions…that comply fully with the rule of law, including the principle of the independence of the judiciary”.

The ICJ’s secretary-general, Santiago Canton, noted that Nawrocki has refused to swear in five of the eight TK judges elected by parliament this year. That “violates international standards and is contrary to the interim measures indicated by the European Court of Human Rights”, said Canton.

In May, the ECHR issued an interim order for all judges elected by parliament to be allowed to serve on the court. However, that has been ignored by Nawrocki and Święczkowski, who argued that the ECHR does not have the authority to make such a decision.

The ICJ also noted that the roots of the crisis at the TK date back a decade, to the time when the PiS government took actions – including unlawfully appointing judges to the tribunal – that rendered the court illegitimate.

 

“At the same time,” continued Canton, “the suspension of the president and vice-president of the tribunal without a fair and appropriate procedure established by law, carried out with the involvement of the police, contravenes international standards on the independence of the judiciary.”

In its statement, the ICJ added that “criminal and disciplinary proceedings must respect all the guarantees of a fair trial and must never be used as a means to change [a court’s] composition”.

Later on Tuesday, after the ICJ had issued its statement, the eight government-backed judges held their first general assembly, at which they moved forward with disciplinary proceedings against Święczkowski and Sochański.

The justice minister, Waldemar Żurek, has also submitted six requests to the TK to lift Święczkowski’s immunity from prosecution so that he can face charges for a range of alleged crimes relating to both his time as chief justice and his previous role as a senior prosecutor under the PiS government.

Skierowałem do Trybunału Konstytucyjnego kolejny, szósty już wniosek o uchylenie immunitetu Bogdanowi Święczkowskiemu, dołączając go do pięciu wniosków przekazanych w piątek. Dzisiejsza sprawa dotyczy zakupu systemu szpiegowskiego Hermes w czasie, gdy pełnił funkcję Prokuratora…

— Waldemar Żurek (@w_zurek) November 3, 2026

The takeover of the TK has also stirred controversy among Polish legal experts. The issue has even caused an unprecedented split at the Helsinki Foundation for Human Rights (HFPC), a well-respected NGO.

On Saturday, the HFPC’s management board issued a statement, signed by its president, Maciej Nowicki, saying that it “sees no clear legal basis” for the actions taken on Friday by the government-backed judges to suspend Święczkowski and take control of the tribunal.

It warned that the situation “set a dangerous precedent” and “does not contribute to fixing the tribunal”. However, HFPC also made clear that the crisis at the court dates back a decade and reiterated its view that Nawrocki “has no right to block or invalidate the election [of judges] by parliament”.

Pełna treść stanowiska: https://t.co/OvJPpaGDel pic.twitter.com/2UpV2itgcd

— Helsińska Fundacja Praw Człowieka (@hfhrpl) October 31, 2026

That statement prompted six of the eight members of HFPC’s council – a separate body from the management board – to resign. Those to depart included a former chief justice of the TK, Andrzej Rzepliński, and a former deputy human rights commissioner, Hanna Machińska.

Machińska announced their resignation in a social media post. She said that the reason for her decision had been the management board’s statement, “with which I disagree”. Speaking later to broadcaster TVN, Machińska said that “we believe that the legal basis [for the TK takeover] was clearly defined”.

Poland’s government, including Prime Minister Donald Tusk, has also argued that the takeover of the tribunal was necessary to ensure that legally appointed judges can take up their seats and that the court’s legitimacy can be restored.

However, on Tuesday evening, Tusk shifted to a more conciliatory tone, offering to hold a one-on-one meeting with Nawrocki to discuss the crisis around the Constitutional Tribunal and “try to find solutions that will protect Poland from any political upheaval”

]]> Disputed Polish constitutional court holds first meeting after takeover by government-backed judges https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/11/03/disputed-polish-constitutional-court-holds-first-meeting-after-takeover-by-government-backed-judges/ Tue, 03 Nov 2026 18:33:46 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=106353

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!

Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.

The group of eight government-backed judges who last week took control of Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) have held a meeting at which they made a number of key decisions, including moving forward with disciplinary proceedings against the court’s chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski.

However, the situation is mired in controversy and uncertainty. Święczkowski and the opposition-aligned president, Karol Nawrocki, do not recognise the judges who are now claiming control of the court, describing their actions as a “coup d’état”.

Meanwhile, there are doubts as to whether today’s general assembly even had a valid quorum, given that the chief justice and six other judges appointed under the former government did not attend.

PILNE: Zgromadzenie Ogólne Sędziów TK przyjęło, że kworum to osiem osóbhttps://t.co/SYEf9Ead3L

— Rzeczpospolita (@rzeczpospolita) November 3, 2026

The meeting was called by Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, who on Friday declared that Święczkowski and the deputy chief justice, Bartłomiej Sochański, had been suspended for failing to fulfil their duties. Korwin-Piotrowska said that she herself, as the longest-serving judge on the court, was taking control.

Large numbers of riot police were deployed outside the court, holding back protesters, including opposition politicians, and preventing Święczkowski and Sochański from entering the court. However, Nawrocki himself did enter the premises, where he clashed physically and verbally with Korwin-Piotrowska.

For a general assembly of the TK to be valid, two thirds of the court’s judges need to be present. Normally, given that the tribunal has 15 positions, that would mean at least 10 judges being present.

However, only eight judges attended today’s meeting. They were all appointed to the TK by the government’s parliamentary majority this year. But Nawrocki has refused to swear in five of them, meaning that their legal status has become disputed.

 

The TK’s seven other judges, including Święczkowski and Sochański, were all appointed to the court under the former Law and Justice (PiS) government, which was widely seen to have brought the court under its political control, including by unlawfully appointing three judges.

None of them attended Tuesday’s general assembly. Nevertheless, the eight judges present at the meeting, which was broadcast live for the first time in the TK’s history, decided that a quorum had been reached.

They did so on the basis that three of the TK’s judges were not authorised to attend: Święczkowski and Sochański, because they are suspended, and Jarosław Wyrembak, because he inherited his position from one of PiS’s unlawfully appointed judges.

That meant only 12 judges were authorised to attend, and two thirds of that number is eight, meaning that a quorum had been reached.

Zgromadzenie Ogólne TK: JEST KWORUM! 👏
Według przedstawionej interpretacji liczy się je od 12 uprawnionych osób. 2/3 × 12 = 8.
Prawo i matematyka.👏 pic.twitter.com/77v2ep9HbT

— Pani Prezes 👠 (@PaniNaSzpilkach) November 3, 2026

Once that issue was agreed, the eight judges present proceeded to decide upon a number of key issues. First, they adopted a draft budget for the TK for 2027, something that Święczkowski had been unable to achieve, which was used as an argument for his ousting.

Second, they drew lots to decide which of the TK’s judges would sit on disciplinary panels for Święczkowski and Sochański in relation to their suspension from the court.

However, some legal experts have expressed doubt as to whether a legal quorum was established at today’s meeting. Ryszard Piotrowski, a prominent constitutional scholar, called the meeting “illegal”, reports news website Onet. Przemysław Rosati, the president of the Supreme Bar Council, also expressed his doubts.

Obniżenie progu kworum na skutek zawieszenia prezesa i wiceprezesa otwiera puszkę Pandory. To jest mechanizm, który pozwala dowolnie obniżać kworum na Zgromadzeniu Ogólnym TK – wystarczy, że prezes zawiesi 10 sędziów i będzie mógł na Zgromadzeniu podejmować decyzję w trzy osoby.…

— Marcin Matczak (@wsamraz) November 3, 2026

Święczkowski himself rejected the legitimacy of what he called a “social gathering”, saying that Korwin-Piotrowska is a “usurper” who has no right to call a general assembly at all, reported Polsat News.

Shortly before the meeting at the TK, Nawrocki also met with the prime minister, Donald Tusk, for the first time since the crisis at the court broke out last Friday. They had convened at the presidential palace for a meeting of the National Security Council that Nawrocki had called before the TK crisis.

During public remarks broadcast before the confidential meeting got underway, Nawrocki accused the government of “illegally taking over the Constitutional Tribunal”. He added that Tusk “bears full responsibility for…all these illegal actions”.

Grubo! Karol Nawrocki do Tuska:

„Pełną odpowiedzialność za wszystkie nielegalne działa w Trybunale Konstytucyjnym ponosi jeden człowiek, który jest obecny – premier Donald Tusk” pic.twitter.com/WMPnWTZIKt

— chrzanik (@chrzanikx) November 3, 2026

Tusk and his government have argued that the source of the crisis is, in fact, Nawrocki’s refusal to swear in judges appointed by parliament, as he is required to do, and then Święczkowski’s resultant refusal to accept those judges onto the court.

They also note that the TK has not been legitimate for a decade, since PiS unlawfully appointed judges and brought the court under its political influence.

Speaking to broadcaster TVN on Tuesday before the general assembly, justice minister Waldemar Żurek said that the actions being undertaken by Korwin-Piotrowska are the only way “to rebuild the independence of the tribunal”.

]]> Poland has EU’s second-highest electricity prices accounting for cost of living https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/11/03/poland-has-eus-second-highest-electricity-prices-accounting-for-cost-of-living/ Tue, 03 Nov 2026 13:27:32 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=106334

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!

Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.

Poland had the second-highest household electricity prices in the European Union in the first half of 2026 after adjusting for differences in the cost of living, new Eurostat data show. Prices in Poland were also among the fastest-rising in the bloc.

Poland’s relatively high electricity costs reflect the country’s continued reliance on coal, which results in EU charges for carbon emissions, and its taxes and levies, which make up the largest share of household electricity bills anywhere in the EU.

In nominal terms, Polish households paid €29.99 per 100 kilowatt-hours (kWh) for electricity in the first half of 2026. This was the seventh-highest price among the EU’s 27 member states and above the bloc-wide average of €28.32.

Ireland (€38.71 per 100 kWh) had the highest prices, followed by Germany (€36.18) and Belgium (€35.75). The lowest costs were recorded in Hungary (€11.39), Malta (€12.68) and Bulgaria (€13.41).

However, when adjusted for purchasing power standards (PPS), which account for differences in the cost of living, Poland ranked second in the EU, at 41.12 PPS per 100 kWh.

Only Romania had higher prices, at 46.89 PPS. The lowest prices when measured in PPS were recorded in Malta (13.75), Hungary (14.7) and Luxembourg (15.47).

Poland’s electricity prices, in PPS terms, rose by 10.7% compared with the second half of 2025, which was the second-biggest increase in the EU after Finland. They were also up 17.6% compared to the first half of 2025, the fourth-largest rise in the bloc.

 

One reason why electricity prices in Poland remain high is the country’s continued reliance on coal, which last year generated just over half of power, by far the highest proportion in the EU.

Almost all coal used in Polish power plants is mined domestically and is among the most expensive in the world to extract. Additionally, burning it also produces high carbon emissions, which power generators must pay for under the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS).

These costs contribute to the high taxes and levies included in household electricity bills, which accounted for 39% of the final price in Poland in the first half of 2026. This was the highest share in the EU, ahead of Germany (23.6%) and well above the bloc-wide average of 18.6%.

“In Poland, only one-third of our electricity generation is carbon-free. We have to pay for the rest – often dearly,” noted Polish energy journalist Jakub Wiech, commenting on the data.

Without taxes and levies, the nominal price of electricity in Poland would have been just under €16 per 100 kWh, below the EU average of €20.27.

However, Bartłomiej Orzeł of the Project Tempo think tank notes that electricity prices in Poland would, in fact, be even higher were it not for the huge state subsidies paid to support the unprofitable coal mining sector, which amount to billions of zloty a year but also shield end consumers from the full cost of extracting coal.

He told news website Interia that mines actually sell coal to power stations at a price below the cost of extraction.

Poland will from next month be the last remaining EU country still mining hard coal, after the Czech Republic – the only other producer – announced the closure of its last mine https://t.co/0sfMDQb19N

According to Wiech, the high tax burden also reflects the costs of transforming Poland’s energy sector while continuing to support coal-fired power stations and the state budget.

Poland’s first-ever nest of Asian hornets, an invasive species seen as a particular threat because it preys on honeybees, has been eliminated. But scientists who have studied the colony say that it is likely more will be found next year.

Since arriving in France in 2004, Asian hornets, which are indigenous to Southeast Asia, have gradually spread to other European countries.

The first confirmed nest to be found in Poland was sighted in a tree in the village of Wielka Wieś near Kraków in mid-October, with individual hornets also being spotted at the apiary of the city’s AGH University of Science and Technology.

The nest was removed last week and sent to be studied by a team of scientists at Wrocław University of Environmental and Life Sciences, reports the Polish Press Agency (PAP).

Paweł Migdał, from the university’s faculty of biology and animal science, told PAP that the nest was “fairly large” considering the Polish climate, containing around 1,000 workers and several dozen queens and males.

The scientists’ assessment of the nest revealed that it contained eggs and larvae, indicating that the hornets inhabiting it were still feeding, he added.

“I think we’ll find more of these nests,” Migdał told PAP. “They’re often built in the treetops, which means they’re invisible until the leaves fall in the autumn.”

Young queens had already left the nest to establish new ones after overwintering, and have greater chances of surviving the longer and warmer the Polish autumn is, he explained. They seek shelter in warm, dry places, such as underground or in storage areas.

 

With queens measuring 30mm and males about 24mm, Asian hornets, also known as the yellow-legged hornet, are smaller than the European variety, and no more dangerous to humans than European hornets or wasps.

The major concern over their arrival relates to their tendency to seek out beehives and prey on honeybees.

“Besides killing honeybees, their presence also causes bees in apiaries to stop working,” explained Migdał. “With the European hornet, the bees recognise the threat but, in a sense, continue working. However, the yellow-legged hornet presents a completely new threat to them.”

The number of bee colonies in Poland has risen 54% over the last decade to reach two million, thanks in part to a state programme supporting beekeepers.

Bees' value to the ecosystem as pollinators is estimated to be worth 5bn zloty (€1.1bn) https://t.co/ElISOc2o2T

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 30, 2022

The scale of the species’ invasiveness is shown by the fact that it releases an average of 150 young queens from its nest, and sometimes even 500 – each of which can potentially create its own nest – while European hornets release just 50, Migdał pointed out.

The location of the first nest found in Poland surprised scientists as the closest previously known was in Opava, around 150 km away in the Czech Republic. The hornets therefore probably travelled in a vehicle, although Migdał noted a potential concern that other populations might be found between the two sites.

He called Nawrocki’s behaviour at the TK “shameful” and said he “hoped prosecutors will take action, because it is unacceptable for someone protected by presidential immunity to behave in such a way”.

Meanwhile, Tusk’s other main coalition partner, The Left (Lewica), announced on Saturday afternoon that it would not attend the talks with Nawrocki.

“One cannot accept an invitation from someone who is himself responsible for the current situation regarding the Constitutional Tribunal,” wrote Anna-Maria Żukowska, the head of The Left’s parliamentary caucus. “The TK is in the hands of independent judges. Politicians should not tell them what to do.”

]]> Chaos at Poland’s constitutional court as government-backed judges seek to oust chief justice https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/10/30/chaos-at-polands-constitutional-court-as-government-backed-judges-seek-to-oust-chief-justice/ Fri, 30 Oct 2026 20:55:24 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=106234

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!

Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.

Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) was plunged into chaos on Friday evening as one group of judges, backed by the government, moved to take control of the court from its chief justice, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition and President Karol Nawrocki.

One of the government-backed judges said that she had suspended the chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, from his duties. Police have surrounded the court and were seen preventing Święczkowski from entering the grounds after his supporters had cut through the fence with a power tool.

Święczkowski and the opposition claim that an illegal “coup d’état” is underway. Nawrocki, who had been flying to Senegal for a state visit, ordered his plane to turn around and return to Warsaw.

Prezes Świeczkowski wraz z grupą posłów przeciął łańcuchy i próbuje dostać się do trybunału konstytucyjnego.

Policja nie chce go przepuścić!

Przecież to bezprawie! pic.twitter.com/XbIXigwIi3

— Jan Molski 🇵🇱 (@JanMolski) October 30, 2026

The dramatic events follow a years-long crisis surrounding the TK. Since the current government – a coalition ranging from left to centre right led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk – came to power in 2023, it has refused to recognise the court’s legitimacy.

That is because three of its judges were unlawfully appointed under the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, which was widely seen to have brought the court under political control.

As a result, Tusk’s government has ignored the TK’s rulings and, until this year, refused to even nominate new judges to fill vacancies that arose on the court’s 15-person bench.

 

That changed in March, when the ruling coalition began filling the backlog of empty seats. So far this year, parliament has chosen eight new judges, meaning that its nominees in theory now have a majority on the court.

However, under Polish law, although new TK judges are chosen by parliament, they must swear an oath “before the president”. Nawrocki, who is aligned with PiS, has refused to swear in five of those eight new judges, citing concerns over how they were chosen or their qualifications.

Those five judges arranged their own swearing-in ceremonies in parliament and submitted their oaths to the president’s office. However, Święczkowski, who before being appointed as a TK judge had served in the former PiS government, refused to accept those five judges on the court.

In doing so, he ignored an order by the European Court of Human Rights that the judges be allowed to take up their positions. Święczkowski argued that the ECHR had no authority to issue such a ruling.

The standoff between the government and president over Poland’s constitutional court deepened today, as Maciej Berek, whom the prime minister recently described as his “right-hand man”, took his oath as a new judge without the presence of the president https://t.co/MrExiJRsEN

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 14, 2026

Rumours have long swirled that the government would introduce those judges onto the court by force. PiS supporters have been camped outside the TK grounds for weeks with the aim of preventing that from happening.

On Friday evening, large numbers of riot police were deployed around the TK. On the court’s website, a brief statement appeared, saying that a “break in the activities” of Święczkowski and his deputy chief justice, Bartłomiej Sochański, had been ordered.

The statement did not say who had ordered that break, but it cited article 130 of the law on common courts, under which the president of a court or the justice minister can order an immediate break in a judge’s official duties if they are caught in the act of committing an offence.

However, Marcin Matczak, a prominent scholar of constitutional law who was also a critic of PiS’s judicial reforms, wrote on social media, that, while the justice minister exercises oversight over common courts, he cannot do so over the TK.

“I consider Bogdan Święczkowski to be the worst person to serve as the president of the TK,” wrote Matczak. “I never thought I’d end up defending him, but this legal basis [for suspending Święczkowski] is nonexistent for a million reasons.”

Ze szczątkowych informacji, na jakiej podstawie zawieszono B. Święczkowskiego, wynika, że ma to być art. 19 ustawy o statusie sędziów TK, który mówi, że do spraw nieuregulowanych w tej ustawie stosuje się „przepisy dotyczące praw i obowiązków sędziów SN” i art. 130 ustawy o SN,…

— Marcin Matczak (@wsamraz) October 30, 2026

Meanwhile, Waldemar Żurek, the justice minister and prosecutor general, issued a statement announcing that he had submitted motions to the TK to waive the immunity from prosecution of Świeczkowski and Sochański.

He said that the documents had been “delivered to the longest-serving judge of the Constitutional Tribunal”.

That was a reference to Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, one of the TK judges whom Nawrocki has refused to swear in. She told state broadcaster TVP that it was she who had issued the order to suspend Święczkowski from his duties.

She justified her action by accusing Święczkowski of blocking judges from taking up their positions and of overseeing irregularities in the assignment of judges to cases, reports Polskie Radio.

Korwin-Piotrowska’s claim to have the longest tenure among TK judges relates not to her service on tribunal itself, but to the fact that she first began her judicial career in 1995.

🗣️ “Bogdan Święczkowski narusza zasady funkcjonowania TK. (…) Nie było innego wyjścia”

– sędzia Anna Korwin-Piotrowska w TVP Info. pic.twitter.com/22FYJJbQAC

— tvp.info 🇵🇱 (@tvp_info) October 30, 2026

While the TK website appears to now be under the control of Korwin-Piotrowska, the court’s account on social media service X issued a statement saying that “an unlawful takeover of the TK’s website has occurred”, that “Bogdan Święczkowski remains chief justice”, and that “Korwin-Piotrowska is not a TK judge”.

“All persons participating in these actions are committing the crime of a coup d’état,” it added.

Nastąpiło bezprawne przejęcie strony internetowej Trybunału Konstytucyjnego.

Prezesem @TK_GOV_PL jest nadal Bogdan Święczkowski, a Wiceprezesem Bartłomiej Sochański.

Pani Anna Korwin-Piotrowska nie jest sędzią Trybunału Konstytucyjnego.

Wszystkie osoby uczestniczące w…

— Trybunał Konstytucyjny (@TK_GOV_PL) October 30, 2026

The court’s spokeswoman, Weronika Ścibor, told broadcaster Kanał Zero that “seven people elected as [TK] judges this year” had been escorted into the building by officers from the State Protection Service (SOP), a body responsible for protecting state officials. SOP is subordinate to the interior minister.

She said they had entered the grounds of the court through a gate that leads from the prime minister’s chancellery, rather than the main entrance from the street where protesters are gathered.

Korwin-Piotrowska also confirmed to TVP that she was one of seven judges who were inside the TK on Friday evening.

Rzeczniczka Trybunału Konstytucyjnego Weronika Ścibor komentuje sytuację w TK.

Według jej relacji siedem osób wybranych na sędziów weszło do budynku w asyście funkcjonariuszy SOP, natomiast wiceprezes Bartłomiej Sochański nie został wpuszczony na teren Trybunału. pic.twitter.com/VwxU4UrYuz

— OficjalneZero (@OficjalneZero) October 30, 2026

The developments at the court prompted outrage from the opposition. PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński declared outside the court that “as of today, Poland has become a police state, and from there it’s a straight path to authoritarianism, and then to totalitarianism”.

Kaczyński called on Nawrocki to return to Poland from his state visit to Senegal and defend the court. The president himself quickly confirmed that he had done so, with flight trackers showing his plane turning around in midair and heading back to Poland.

Meanwhile, Zbigniew Kapiński, the chief justice of the Supreme Court – a separate entity from the Constitutional Tribunal – told Kanał Zero that he was “appalled” by what was happening, which was “undoubtedly a coup d’état”.

Our most tracked flight right now: A Polish government aircraft en route to Senegal is now returning to Warsaw. https://t.co/YdLhQmV8pl pic.twitter.com/Dz9KPgI3eI

— Flightradar24 (@flightradar24) October 30, 2026

Tusk, however, issued a statement on social media defending what was taking place at the TK.

“Restoring the rule of law is our duty,” he wrote. “After years of PiS-led lawlessness, this is a difficult process, sometimes painful, and it requires decisive action. There is no other way.”

Poland has introduced its first fast-track zones for renewable energy projects as the coal-dependent country seeks to speed up its transition to cleaner sources of electricity.

The regional assembly in Wielkopolska province, western Poland, this week approved plans covering 105.4 hectares across four municipalities, where investors will be able to develop solar farms under simplified planning and environmental procedures.

The environment ministry estimates that the changes, introduced under an EU directive, could reduce project preparation times from three to four years down to just one or two years.

Pierwsze #OPRO już są! Sejmik województwa wielkopolskiego przyjął dziś pierwsze w Polsce plany OPRO. Obejmą one ok. 105,4 ha w gminach Lwówek, Rawicz, Słupca i Złotów.🔆

❓Czym jest OPRO?
✅To Obszary Przyspieszonego Rozwoju #OZE, czyli tereny, na których – już podczas ich…

— Marek Pogorzelski (@rzeczni_MKiS) October 26, 2026

Under the scheme, planning and much of the environmental assessment will be completed before investors apply for permits, allowing projects to move forward more quickly.

Environmental authorities will also have a maximum of 45 days to review projects with a capacity of at least 150 kW. Industry representatives told energy Świat OZE, a renewable energy news service, that obtaining an environmental decision can currently take up to 150 days.

The newly designated areas, known as Accelerated Renewable Energy Development Zones (OPRO), will be located in the municipalities of Złotów, Lwówek, Rawicz and Słupca. Together, they have an estimated technical potential of 66-80 megawatts of solar capacity, depending on the arrangement of the panels.

Maria Niewitała-Rej, a climate and energy policy analyst at the Reform Institute, a Warsaw-based think tank, told the Dziennik Gazeta Prawna newspaper that while “the scale of the Wielkopolska plan is modest, the adoption of the first resolutions is a step in the right direction”.

 

The creation of accelerated renewable energy development zones stems from the EU’s revised Renewable Energy Directive (RED III), which requires member states to designate areas where renewable energy projects can be developed more quickly.

Under the directive, permitting procedures in these zones should take no longer than 12 months for onshore projects and 24 months for offshore projects.

EU rules required the first zones to be designated by 21 February 2026, making Poland’s adoption several months late.

Polish state mining firm JSW, which is the EU's largest producer of coking coal and one of Poland's biggest employers, has announced that it will cut over 4,000 jobs, 21% of its workforce, by the end of this year as it seeks to stem large financial losses https://t.co/EWP3rAVMaH

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 2, 2026

Poland has long had one of Europe’s most polluting energy sectors. The country still produces around half of its electricity from coal, by far the higher proportion in the EU.

However, the share of renewables has grown significantly in recent years. It nearly doubled from 14.7% of the energy mix in 2021 to 29.4% in 2025. Onshore wind was the largest contributor last year, accounting for 14.2%, followed by solar at 12.1% and biomass at 1.8%.

Poland’s national energy and climate plan, approved in June, envisages coal accounting for just 0-5% of the energy mix by 2040. Around 15-16% will come from nuclear, 7-8% from gas, with most of the rest from renewables: onshore wind (22-27%), offshore wind (18-21%) and solar (14-18%).

The Left, a junior partner in Poland’s ruling coalition, has proposed a bill to abolish the Church Fund, which provides state subsidies for the health insurance contributions of clergy. It says it is frustrated by delays in fulfilling a pledge made by most parties in the wide ruling coalition to reform the fund.

However, another coalition partner, the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL), says that it will oppose the bill, calling instead for a system allowing taxpayers to allocate part of their taxes to religious institutions of their choice. Senior church figures also say they have not been consulted.

📣 Lewica składa ustawę likwidującą Fundusz Kościelny. Czas na realizację umowy koalicyjnej w zakresie świeckiego państwa‼️

Co zakłada nasz projekt? ⬇️

✅ Składki na duchownych przestają być w 80 procentach finansowane z budżetu państwa jak dotychczas. 50% składek pokrywać… pic.twitter.com/syqUMdCugr

— Lewica (@__Lewica) October 29, 2026

The Church Fund, originally established in 1950 to compensate religious communities for property seized by the communist authorities, provides state subsidies for the health insurance contributions of clergy, for religious organisations’ charitable activities, and for the renovation of religious buildings.

It now supports all legally recognised religious denominations in Poland, including those that did not lose property at the time. Last year, the state spent 275.7 million zloty on the Church Fund. This year it has budgeted 272.6 million zloty.

Most of this money is then used to cover 80% of clergy members’ social security contributions. Under the bill proposed by The Left, churches would pay half of the contributions, with clergy covering the other half.

For regular workers, such contributions are funded jointly by employees and their employers, Anna Maria Żukowska, the head of The Left’s parliamentary caucus, pointed out, as quoted by the Polish Press Agency (PAP). “We are introducing the same arrangement for priests and members of the clergy.”

At least 17.5bn zloty in state funds went to religious bodies from 2021-23, with over 95% going to Catholic organisations, the state auditor has found.

In response, the speaker of parliament has proposed measures to reduce and better oversee such spending https://t.co/IN3dpY4La2

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 16, 2025

An exception is made in the bill for members of enclosed religious orders and missionaries, who would have their contributions paid in full by their churches. The cost of maintaining historic churches would be covered by the National Fund for the Protection of Monuments, Żukowska explained.

Włodzimierz Czarzasty, who is the leader of The Left as well as the speaker of the Sejm, the more powerful chamber in the Polish parliament, said the party did not oppose religion but wanted clergy to be treated equally under the law.

“I would like to remind my coalition partners: our coalition agreement includes a commitment to work toward establishing the principles of a secular state in Poland,” he said, speaking alongside Żukowska. “Our patience is running out”.

 

Ahead of the 2023 election, both the centrist Civic Coalition (KO) led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk and The Left pledged to abolish the Church Fund, while the centre-right Poland 2050 (Polska 2050) proposed replacing state funding with voluntary taxpayer contributions. PSL had no equivalent formal party-wide pledge.

In 2024, after the coalition came to power, Tusk announced plans to reform the fund and appointed a government working group led by the PSL leader and deputy prime minister, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz. The group’s work has since stalled.

Kosiniak-Kamysz yesterday dismissed The Left’s proposal, saying it has “not the slightest chance of support in parliament”. His party, the second largest in the coalition with 32 of 239 MPs, sees the existing fund as an inexpensive form of compensation and will oppose abolishing it, he vowed.

Instead, taxpayers should be able to allocate part of their taxes to a religious institution of their choice, a system used in several European countries, to “let the Polish people themselves decide whether or not they want to contribute,” he said, quoted by broadcaster Polsat News.

Interior minister Marcin Kierwiński, a member of Tusk’s Civic Coalition (KO), said that he supported reform, but criticised The Left for submitting the bill without consulting its coalition partners.

A long-term decline in trust in the Catholic church in Poland has accelerated over the last year, with only 35% of Poles now saying they trust the church.

Meanwhile, the armed forces now enjoy record-high trust of 94% https://t.co/ErCBE4HwWR

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 17, 2025

Religious communities also criticised the proposal for not having been discussed with them in advance.

In a press statement sent to PAP, the Polish Episcopal Conference (KEP), the main organ of the Catholic church in Poland, said any solution should comply with the country’s agreement with the Vatican, as well as the constitutional principle that relations between the state and religious communities be regulated by mutual agreement.

Bishop Jerzy Samiec, head of the Evangelical-Augsburg Church in Poland, the country’s biggest Protestant body, pointed to the significant costs churches face in maintaining their properties, including care homes and other facilities.

The Catholic Church, Poland’s dominant religious institution, has seen a long-term decline in public trust, with only 35% of Poles saying they trusted it in 2025. That has coincided with a series of crises in recent years, in particular over revelations of child sexual abuse by members of the clergy and negligence in dealing with them by the church hierarchy.

A variety of surveys, including from the church itself, show that religious attendance and identification have been declining in Poland in recent years.

A growing number of Poles are turning away from the Catholic church, but not from religious belief itself.

This creates challenges for the church, but also for Polish identity, which has historically been linked to Catholicism, writes Katarzyna Skiba https://t.co/udWGzd0X7F

City AM https://www.cityam.com/ London's Business Newspaper Wed, 04 Nov 2026 19:58:03 +0000 en-GB hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.4 https://www.cityam.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/app_launcher_icon_final_rounded.png?w=32 City AM https://www.cityam.com/ 32 32 213406410 Andy Burnham says stockpile beans and tuna: Here’s the wine to pair with that https://www.cityam.com/andy-burnham-says-stockpile-beans-and-tuna-heres-the-wine-to-pair-with-that/ Wed, 04 Nov 2026 18:58:04 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2474656

Elevate emergency tins with wine pairings: sparkling rosé for beans, Riesling for tuna and Valpolicella for corned beef—discover what to pour.]]>

Andy Burnham has advised us to stock up on tinned goods and bottled water for at least three days, but when you are hunkered up at home facing Armageddon then a bottle of Evian isn’t going to lift anyone’s spirits. Here are the wines that can transform a sad can into fine cuisine. 

Heinz Baked Beans x Sparkling Rosé

The number one tinned product in any British kitchen. We eat more beans in the UK than the rest of the world put together, with over a whopping two million cans consumed every single day. You may enjoy them over a baked potato, on your morning toast or cold straight from the can, like English acting royalty Joanna Lumley. But finding something to pair with that sweet, tangy tomato sauce is a tricky thing to get right. 

When faced with dining dilemmas there are two wines that usually work: rosé and sparkling. These are pairing failsafes because of their fruitiness and freshness. Provence’s Sparkling Roseblood d’Estoublon combines both (£27, bottlesbygoedhuiswaddesdon.com) with a delightful red berry effervescence to buoy the beans. 

Cream of Chicken Soup x Beaujolais Blanc

Technically, cream of tomato is the more popular choice but chicken comes a close second and, as it contains more protein, it’s a better option for “healthy” long life soups. Ideally you want a white wine with some stone fruits to compliment the chicken and some acidity to cut through the cream. Chateau d’Emeringes Beaujolais Villages Blanc 2024 (£11.50, The Wine Society) is unoaked, old vine chardonnay with zip, zest and elegance. 

Tinned Tuna x Dry Riesling

Tinned fish is a brilliant option to get your proteins and omegas in, and while sardines are coasting a wellness trend right now, tuna is by far the most popular fish, selling more than all other tinned seafood options combined. Whether you go for olive oil or brine, it is a versatile household staple. Bring those fresh seafood flavours to the fore with a bright, crisp white wine. Yalumba Y Series Riesling (£12.50, Ocado) is a brilliant dry white with layered flavours and real citrus pep. The Y Series Sauvignon Blanc (£17.49, Tesco) is a reliable choice too.  

Corned Beef x Valpolicella 

I had to buy my first tin of corned beef to experiment with this. Miles told MPs on the Treasury Committee that so-called stealth taxes, which mean the Treasury is getting billions of pounds more than it would have done if thresholds moved up with inflation each, limited improvements in living standards. 

The OBR economist said stealth taxes were one of the three main factors slowing household disposable income growth, behind low GDP per capita figures since the Great Financial Crisis and a recent increase in energy prices. 

Money coming straight out of disposable income

He said a lack of productivity growth had been “unusually low for an extended period now”, adding that GDP per person would be about 30 per cent higher had growth in the UK economy continued at the same pace as it had done before the 2008 crisis.

He added: “And then there’s an ongoing increase in the overall effective tax rate in the UK, and much of that comes because of the freeze on thresholds where people move into higher rates of income tax. 

“It’s increasing the average tax take out of people’s income that comes straight out of disposable income.”

The future of UK living standards partly depended on how much longer a freeze on thresholds would continue for, according to Miles. 

Former Chancellor Jeremy Hunt first announced the freeze at the Spring Budget of 2021, saying it would be re-linked to inflation from 2026. In the statement, Hunt also reduced the additional 45 per cent rate threshold to £125,140. In the year after, Hunt extended the freeze through to April 2028 rather than 2026. 

In her first Budget, Rachel Reeves said she would not extend the freeze beyond 2028 in what was then seen as a surprise announcement. However, Reeves U-turned on the commitment as a further extension to April 2031 was her main revenue-raiser in her bid to fund public services and meet fiscal rules. 

Researchers at the Resolution Foundation said the 2020s would be a “catastrophic” decade for living standards. 

Its research showed that, in the 2020s, real household disposable income was set to rise by just 1.4 per cent. 

This is dwarfed by a 28 per cent rise in the ‘90s, an increase of 18 per cent in the noughties, and 14 per cent in the 2010s.

In his appearance before MPs on Wednesday afternoon, Miles suggested there was no imminent escape for the government as “it’s very difficult to move the dial that much through policy”. 

The economist said the government would have to get “an awful lot of good luck” for living standards forecasts to radically improve, though growth boosts from AI or a dramatic fall in energy costs could improve British families’ fortunes.

It may not be as glamorous as performative rule-cutting, but the Financial Services and Markets Bill has the potential to speed up the FCA, write Omar Salem and James Borley 

The British famously love queuing. And remember the outcry when some were accused of jumping the queue to see Queen Elizabeth II lying in state? Queuing isn’t just a tradition but says something about our sense of fairness.  

But we have all been in a situation where the queue isn’t moving, no one knows what’s happening and we start thinking about giving up. Too often that is the case for applicants for FCA and PRA licences, some of whom may go to other countries. 

Ask anyone who has tried to launch a payments firm or buy a broker what slows them down, and the answer is rarely the rules. It is the wait – unsure when the regulator will decide, or even when it will start deciding.

Granted, things have improved from the backlogs of a few years ago, and the FCA has become more proactive in explaining the process and its expectations to the market, but the process still takes too long and lacks accountability. 

The regulators’ favourite loophole

A key example of the lack of regulatory accountability in the system is the, at best, liberal interpretation of the law that the regulators have been using to massage their performance statistics. 

The clock for regulators to decide an application only starts ticking when it is ‘complete’. ‘Incomplete’ has become a convenient way for the FCA and PRA to buy more time, regardless of whether it is warranted or not. 

To complicate things further, the FCA also says it can choose to treat an application as ‘not been received’ because it does not include the ‘minimum information’ required. So, what is the difference between an application rejected for not having the ‘minimum information’ and one that is incomplete? Yes, you’re not alone in being confused.

The bill we need

The Financial Services and Markets Bill, which is currently making its way through Parliament, would make some limited decreases to deadlines that the regulators need to meet. This is part of the government’s ‘growth agenda’ and efforts to cut red tape. The bill would cut the maximum period for determining an authorisation from a year to… 10 months. The incompleteness loophole would be retained. We can do much better.

For starters, the bill should go further on deadlines and bring approvals for M&A within them. There is no reason why a maximum six-month period to determine an authorisation application should not be possible. The bill should set clearer standards that can’t be gamed on when an application is complete, while letting regulators more easily turn away poor-quality applications quickly.

The FCA should also be encouraged to learn from the firms it authorises. A single application can involve the applicant, its lawyers, several case officers and specialist teams at the FCA. Fintechs coordinate exactly this kind of multi-party work every day, using project management tools such as Jira to assign tasks, track dependencies and show everyone where things stand. Why can’t the FCA do this?

Imagine an applicant able to see that its file is with the financial crime team, that two questions are outstanding and that a decision is on track. Fewer chasing emails, fewer surprises and a clear record of where delays arise that can be used to find ways to improve the process. Agentic AI opens even more possibilities. The bill should require the regulators to report to Parliament on how they are making authorisations more efficient, including by using technology.

Fairness not favours

While there can be a trade-off between risk and growth, there are also many steps the FCA could take to support growth without increasing risk. Faster and more consistent authorisations are a prime example of this. This isn’t about lowering the standard of applications or giving favours to the City, but building a system that works. It may not be as glamorous as performative rule-cutting, but it would make a difference. What is more, like queuing, an accountable and effective authorisations process is a matter of fairness. 

Omar Salem is a partner consultant at Pierson Ferdinand UK LLP. James Borley is director for payment services and digital assets at Complyport

Thousands of UK workers are set to face an effective 64 per cent tax rate on their cash savings under a fresh tax raid launched by John Healey in his maiden Budget.

The Chancellor confirmed he will hike taxes on savings by a further two per cent in April 2027, taking the rate to 44 per cent and 49 per cent for higher and additional rate taxpayers respectively.

He also maintained the frozen tax thresholds implemented by his predecessor Rachel Reeves, including the longstanding personal allowance taper. If a worker’s income exceeds £100,000 the tax-free personal allowance is reduced by £1 for every £2 earned over the limit.

For employees paying 40 per cent income tax on their salary, this clawback adds a further 20p of tax for every £1 of interest received. 

Brits caught in the taper pay an effective 60 per cent marginal rate on savings interest above their allowance, but the incoming tax hike will see this penalty rise to 64 per cent.

Tax trap paradox

For Britain’s highest earners the measure creates far less distortion compared to those who find themselves close to the threshold.

Workers earning £200,000 have their personal allowance completely wiped out by their salary alone. This means additional savings interest cannot trigger any further tax clawback, leaving them to be taxed solely at the flat 49 per cent rate.

Instead workers on the lower end of the bracket, typically dubbed high earners not rich yet (HENRYs) are instead expected to bear the brunt of the increase.

HENRYs earning £110,000 land directly in the taper zone with a £500 personal savings allowance.

Every pound of savings interest above the £500 triggers the 44 per cent higher-rate savings tax while simultaneously stripping away 50p of their personal allowance.

The lost allowance exposes an extra 50p of salary to 40 per cent income tax, creating the “punishing” 64 per cent effective marginal rate and putting the rate they face 15 percentage points higher than someone earning nearly double their pay.

Michael Healy, chief executive of IG consumer, said: “The £100,000 threshold has become one of the most punishing features of Britain’s tax system. 

“Years of frozen thresholds have dragged more working professionals into its grip, and the Chancellor has now tightened the squeeze.”

Childcare cliff edge

The tax hike puts further pressure on HENRYs, including those who have lost their free childcare hours upon surpassing the £100,000 earnings threshold.

In dual households, individual salaries are taken into account meaning childcare hours are taken the moment one parent crosses the £100,000 line regardless of what the other earns.

Over 90 per cent who have crossed the threshold have argued it has left them unable to build long-term wealth or invest, according to IG.

More than half said they would invest more if crossing the threshold did not cost them free childcare.

“Higher taxes on savings risk undermining efforts to encourage more people to invest,” said Healy.

“Families already struggling with punitive tax rates and the loss of childcare support will have even less disposable income to put towards building long-term wealth. The result is a tax system that makes it harder for people to get ahead financially.”

Shabana Mahmood’s climbdown will cost taxpayers billions and entrench state overreach, says Rakib Ehsan

While home secretary Shabana Mahmood’s climbdown over her settlement reforms will delight some within her own party, it will disappoint many who believed that the Burnham Government would address growing public concerns over sensitive matters of immigration, integration, and identity.

Mahmood’s initial plans for migrant care workers already in the UK to wait 15 years for permanent settlement were previously labelled by former deputy prime minister and current housing secretary as “un-British”, with energy secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh hesitating to express support for the reforms in a recent interview. Under the watered-down plans, if care workers earn at least £25,000 a year and entered the UK before May 2025, they will be eligible for indefinite leave to remain (ILR) after five years – sparing 282,000 migrants from delayed settlement.

Quality and quantity

The climbdown will not only reinforce public anxieties over the lack of quantity and quality control when it comes to the UK’s lax immigration system – it is likely to cost British taxpayers billions of pounds. Having ILR, migrants gain a suite of rights and benefits, such as being able to work without restrictions and having access to public funds. Moving from ‘pre-settled status’ to having ILR means that migrants may become eligible to apply for social housing (on the grounds of meeting the council’s requirements based on length of residency in the local authority area and need). Migrants with ILR are exempt from paying the Immigration Health Surcharge (HIS), therefore entitled to free access to NHS hospital treatment on a similar basis to that of an ordinarily resident person. A variety of welfare benefits are available with ILR (with conditions depending on the type of state assistance), as well as council tax reductions. Mahmood is currently refusing to specify how much scrapping her plan to make foreign care workers already in the UK wait longer to qualify for permanent settlement will cost.

There is also the worry that reversing the decision to extend the period before migrant care workers qualify for ILR, means that the UK Government is unwilling to implement a comprehensive skills, training and pay strategy for the sector to make jobs more attractive for domestic workers. As Policy Exchange argued in its Double Vision report in relation to medics, the UK must stop relying so heavily on overseas recruitment and should instead focus on finding ways to attract domestic workers into healthcare professions. 

The reality is that care roles are both mentally challenging and physically demanding. As it stands, British citizens who are entertaining entering the care professions are simply not provided with the training support, sufficient pay, and favourable working conditions they deserve – ultimately because the sector has been flooded with foreign care workers who are generally accepting of low wages and superficial rights. There are also questions regarding the overall level of English language proficiency among migrant workers who arrived after the January 2021 post-Brexit liberalisation of visa rules – which in turn feeds into concerns over the quality of care for service users, especially elderly people who speak specific local dialects. The reckless internationalisation of care in the country is a national scandal.

But there is a broader-picture problem here – what kind of state do we have and what type of society do we now live in? One of the most pro-family measures any government could take is phasing out care visas completely. The sorry model of private care homes profiting from a cultural individualism where familial caring responsibilities are outsourced to cheap foreign labour should be rejected – especially by a Labour government with a supposedly socially conservative home secretary. Instead, it has now been consolidated by the state. The current government has missed a golden opportunity to send a signal that the UK is committed to a national care approach centred on a motivated domestic workforce and the encouragement of within-the-family support except for the very most serious mental and physical conditions.

Dr Rakib Ehsan is a senior fellow at Policy Exchange.

    HMRC is actively writing to limited liability partnerships (LLPs) as firms race to reassess their members’ tax status after the landmark legal ruling, even as both sides “hold their cards close to their chests.”

    Members of an LLP are treated as self-employed partners, meaning they don’t pay the 15 per cent employer’s national insurance contributions on their pay. In order for firms to avoid tax by just naming staff as ‘partners’, the salaried member rule was put into place. Under this rule, a member is legally deemed an employee for tax purposes unless they don’t meet at least one of three specific conditions.

    But in July, the Supreme Court delivered the first major ruling on how these conditions work in practice in a case against hedge fund Bluecrest Capital Management, founded by the UK’s wealthiest financier, as the taxman successfully argued that the firm’s portfolio managers were functionally employees.

    The decision threw a spanner into the LLP model and emboldened the tax agency.

    The broader professional services sector, a major user of the LLP model, is now under HMRC’s scrutiny.

    Are partners acting as genuine business operators?

    Adam Craggs, partner at RPC, said: “We have in recent months been contacted by a number of substantial professional services firms following the Supreme Court’s decision.”

    Miles Dean, managing director at Andersen UK, explained that the taxman will be looking at “whether individuals described as partners are genuinely operating as business owners or are, in reality, highly paid employees dressed up in partnership clothing.”

    But because the issue is sensitive and firms may be exposed, Sue Robinson, principal in Ryan’s employment tax practice, said LLPs are “keeping [their] cards close to [their] chest”, and HMRC did not want to appear to be attacking LLPs across the board.

    It was recently revealed that Boston Consulting Group disclosed in its public accounts that HMRC is inquiring into the firm over whether its partners are technically self-employed or employees, prompting the consultancy firm to write in its accounts that it sought external legal counsel.

    Labour’s tax gap drive

    As part of Labour’s ‘Close the Tax Gap’ initiative, HMRC has been provided with additional resources to collect unpaid tax.

    The Bluecrest case was worth £200m in tax fees, plus legal fees. For those who are found to be aligned in a similar way, Dean said: “The potential financial exposure is enormous”.

    Craggs explained HMRC’s core predictive analytics tool, Connect, is likely to be the primary tool for this filtering process as it “ingests billions of data points from diverse sources, allowing HMRC to cross-reference data across multiple entities instantly”.

    But the process will be slow, as Robinson explained; HMRC has to take this on a case-by-case basis.

    As Dean added, “There is a danger of painting all LLPs with the same brush.” He explained that there “are legitimate and widely used business structures, and the distinction between genuine partners and salaried members is not always straightforward.”

    When approached for a comment, an HMRC spokesperson said: “The Supreme Court’s decision provided helpful clarity on how the salaried member rules should be implemented. We want to make sure everyone gets their right tax, and we are considering if any updates should be made to our online guidance to help them do this.”

For about five months, a browser extension sat quietly on the home computers of 154 people and watched them log in.

The researchers never saw a password. Everything was hashed on the machine before it went anywhere, leaving them with the shape of each one: its length, its mix of characters, the site it was typed into, and whether the same string had appeared before.

Very often, it had.

What 154 people actually typed

Sarah Pearman and her co-authors at Carnegie Mellon University presented the results at a 2017 computer security conference, having followed each participant for an average of 147 days. Those people logged in across 26 web domains apiece and covered the lot with fewer than 10 distinct passwords.

Roughly 60 per cent of those distinct passwords were recycled, either typed identically on another site or built around a chunk of four or more characters lifted from one the same person used elsewhere.

Banking got no special treatment. Around 85 per cent of the passwords on financial sites appeared elsewhere too, and nearly all of that crossover ran into unrelated categories, so the login for a savings account was also the login for a shoe shop.

What partial reuse looks like up close

Mostly it looks like adding a character.

Among passwords that shared a substring with another, the most common gap between the two was a single character. Digits were the strongest predictor in the Carnegie Mellon model, multiplying the odds of reuse by more than twelve. The authors’ own explanation is that a password with a number in it satisfies more websites’ fussy signup rules, so it travels further.

The tidy minority had barely any accounts

Ten participants mostly built something new for each site, which sounds like a win for good habits until you look at what they were doing online. With one exception, every one of them entered passwords on eight domains or fewer, and they were active on their computers on only 17 per cent of the days they spent enrolled.

The heavy users went the other way. Ninety-four participants, the largest cluster by far, both copied passwords outright and modified them, and they averaged 32 online accounts each. Discipline held up fine at eight accounts and collapsed at thirty.

The password manager result, with a handbrake

Only 19 of the 154 participants had a password manager installed, and the study found no measurable effect on either reuse or strength.

That result deserves caution. One paper is one paper, the subgroup is tiny, and the software could not tell whether people were generating random strings or merely parking passwords they had invented themselves. Rick Wash and colleagues at Michigan State University, who watched 134 participants over six weeks, found each password being reused on 1.7 to 3.4 websites. Their study did not measure partial reuse at all, so the higher figure out of Pittsburgh partly reflects counting a habit nobody had counted before.

Somewhere there is a text file with an old forum password in it, sitting in a folder alongside a few hundred million others. Troy Hunt, the Australian security researcher behind the breach notification service Have I Been Pwned, has documented the trade in combo lists, which are exactly that: vast dumps of email and password pairs scraped out of past breaches. Cheap automated tools fire them at unrelated websites until one opens. Defending against it is awkward, because a successful run looks identical to a customer logging in correctly.

One shared string, and the breach at a defunct hobby forum becomes a problem at an email provider.

The rules that encouraged this have been withdrawn

In 2025, the US National Institute of Standards and Technology finalised revision 4 of its digital identity guidelines, and the password section reads like a quiet apology. Websites must stop demanding mixtures of character types, and they must stop forcing periodic changes unless there is evidence of compromise. Password managers and autofill have to be allowed, and every new password gets checked against blocklists of strings already known to have leaked.

Each of those requirements targets the behaviour the extension recorded: a handful of memorable strings, nudged sideways by a digit, stretched across an entire online life.

The standard now assumes a machine is doing the remembering. Anyone who ever stuck a “1” on the end to get past a signup form was just covering the shift until it arrived.

A camera that stayed switched off cost a Florida software company about 75,000 euros.

It belonged to a telemarketer working from the small Dutch town of Diessen, employed since January 2019 by Chetu, an American software firm that at the time ran a Dutch office in Rijswijk. On 23 August 2022 he was told to join something called the Corrective Action Program, which meant staying logged in for his whole shift, sharing his screen and leaving his laptop camera on. He shared the screen. The camera stayed dark.

His objection was brief and entirely unlegalistic. Court filings quoted by The Register record him saying he was not comfortable being monitored for nine hours a day, calling it “an invasion of my privacy” and noting that his laptop activity was already visible to management.

Two more instructions followed, each firmer than the last. On 26 August he was dismissed on the spot, the stated reasons being refusal to work and insubordination.

Three days from the first instruction to the sack.

What the company argued

Chetu’s case, set out in the published judgment of the Court of Zeeland-West-Brabant, was that watching a remote worker through a webcam is no different from a manager walking past a desk. Performance software already sat on the man’s laptop, and that was not considered enough. Chetu wanted to see him working.

What the judge decided

Ruling on 28 September 2022, the subdistrict judge in Tilburg found that ordering an employee to keep a camera running for a full shift conflicted with his right to respect for private life, and that nothing had been offered to justify it. An unreasonable instruction cannot be unreasonably refused, so there had been no refusal to work and no grounds for summary dismissal.

Data protection law dropped out early. On the understanding that no footage would be recorded, stored or used for anything, the judge treated the monitoring as falling outside data processing altogether, and tested it directly against Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, alongside Strasbourg case law holding that filming staff at work, covert or not, is a serious intrusion into private life. Had the images been kept, the analysis would have looked quite different.

One much-quoted line deserves care. Coverage including a report in Fortune presented the claim that all-day camera tracking is disproportionate and not allowed in the Netherlands as a finding of the court. In the Dutch record it sits among the employee’s own submissions. What the judge actually held was narrower, and sufficient: this instruction, to this man, in his own home, breached Article 8 with no justification advanced.

Why the sum was so large

Almost none of the money was a penalty for the privacy breach. The largest slice, 50,000 euros, was a billijke vergoeding, an equitable award Dutch judges reserve for employers whose conduct in ending a job has been seriously culpable, with a wrongful summary dismissal among the standard triggers, as the Amsterdam employment firm Workx Advocaten explains. Privacy is why the sacking failed. The sacking is what got billed.

Around that sat roughly 8,375 euros for ignoring the notice period, close to 9,500 euros in statutory transition payment, more than 2,700 euros in unpaid wages, 23 days of untaken leave, the 8 per cent holiday allowance and some 585 euros in costs, all itemised by NL Times. His non-compete clause was lifted as well, leaving him free to walk to a competitor.

Is this a bizarre one-off or a policy plenty of people are quietly living with? A survey of 1,000 business leaders at mostly remote companies, commissioned by ResumeBuilder in March 2023, found 37 per cent required staff to sit on a live video feed, and that 93 per cent of those firms had somebody monitoring it, usually for four hours or more a day.

The same survey found 73 per cent had dismissed workers on the strength of monitoring data, and 69 per cent had lost staff who would not accept it.

One survey is one survey. It polled American executives, it relied on self-reporting, and executives describing their own management habits are not a neutral instrument. Treat it as a temperature reading rather than a census.

Where the line actually falls

Whatever this settles, it settles in one jurisdiction, on one set of facts, at the lowest rung of the court system. Article 8 offers nothing in Florida, where employment is generally at will and can end without a stated reason, subject to the usual exceptions for discrimination, retaliation and whatever a contract says.

What the case supplies is a price tag on a boundary that remote-work policy has been drifting across without much thought: supervising the work is one thing, keeping a lens open in somebody’s house for the length of a shift is another. A Dutch judge has now looked at that question once, and the employer left lighter.

Markus Villig was 19 in 2013, fresh out of high school in Tallinn, and frustrated with how hard it was to get a reliable taxi in his own city. He borrowed €5,000 from his family to build a first version of an app, then did the unglamorous part himself: walking up to taxi drivers on the street in Tallinn and persuading them, one at a time, to sign up. What Bolt actually is today looks very different from what Villig built in 2013. Ride-hailing still accounts for the large majority of its revenue, 82 percent in 2024, according to figures reported in public company profiles of Bolt, but the company has spent the years since methodically bolting on new verticals, largely by copying its own playbook of arriving in a category cheaper and faster than the incumbent. Bolt Food launched in Tallinn in August 2019 and now operates in more than 80 cities across 20 countries with over 30,000 partner restaurants. Estonia’s population stood at 1,360,745 at the start of 2026, according to Statistics Estonia. That is smaller than many single cities. Out of it has come ten companies that reached a billion-dollar valuation at some point in their history, among them Skype, Wise, Bolt, Pipedrive, Playtech and Veriff, according to Invest in Estonia’s own tally.

Using CB Insights’ underlying company data alongside that population figure, a figure Invest in Estonia and outlets including Fintech Baltic put at roughly 7.1 unicorns per million residents, based on Invest in Estonia’s cumulative count of companies that have ever reached $1B — not a live ranking CB Insights itself publishes, second only to Liechtenstein and more than three times the United States’ rate of about 2.2 per million.

The tiger leap that came before the unicorns

This density didn’t happen by accident, and it didn’t start with a startup. In 1996, five years after regaining independence from the Soviet Union, Estonia launched a state programme called Tiigrihüpe, or Tiger Leap, championed by future president Toomas Hendrik Ilves and education minister Jaak Aaviksoo. Its goal was blunt: wire the country’s schools for computers and the internet as a deliberate act of catching up. It worked faster than almost anyone expected.

The rollout was rapid but not instantaneous. Education Estonia says all schools had computers by 2000 and all were connected to the internet by 2001. That pattern, alumni from one successful company seeding the next, is common in tech clusters generally, but it is unusually visible in a country as small as Estonia, where the total pool of experienced software engineers was never large to begin with, and where a handful of Skype veterans and their networks touch a disproportionate share of what came after. It wasn’t only talent that recirculated. Toivo Annus, one of Skype’s founding engineers who led its engineering team until the eBay sale, went on to co-found Ambient Sound Investments with three other early Skype engineers in 2003, a private investment firm that has since backed more than 50 early-stage ventures, according to documented accounts of his career. Annus died in 2020, but the firm he helped start is still one of the more active early-stage investors operating out of Tallinn, another channel through which Skype’s original payout kept funding whatever came next.

The ecosystem underneath those ten companies is larger and more active than the unicorn count alone suggests.
